title: Missing lawmakers
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
FOLLOWING the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP on Oct 11, many lawmakers of the PTI remain untraceable. The matter has been raised in parliament and in the courts. During a hearing of related petitions in the Peshawar High Court yesterday, PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan said that 12 MNAs and 14 MPAs belonging to the KP Assembly had been “picked up”. Soon after the proclamation of emergency, Federal Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry had confirmed that KP’s non-functional Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and some members of his cabinet were in “preventive custody”. Meanwhile, on Monday, PTI lawmakers in the National Assembly demanded production orders for their fellow party MNAs. Opposition Leader Mahmood Achakzai endorsed the demand, while Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, raised the issue in the Upper House. One PTI MNA has been arrested at his madressah in Bannu, but the whereabouts of most of the missing lawmakers remain unknown, with their families also in the dark. Some lawmakers have reportedly been in detention since before Oct 11.
This is not the first time that opposition lawmakers in Pakistan have gone ‘missing’. The proclamation of emergency should not, however, mean holding fundamental rights in abeyance. Whether it is members of the assemblies, or ordinary citizens, the Constitution — if that document still holds any value for the wielders of power — guarantees due process to every Pakistani. Therefore, Mr Afridi, as well as other PTI lawmakers, must be produced before the courts forthwith. The state must announce publicly what they are accused of, so that they can defend themselves, and engage counsel of their choice. Mr Chaudhry had said that if there are cases against the PTI leaders they would be charged, and if no evidence is found against them they would be released. The state must keep its promise, and also grant the lawmakers access to their families. Members of the ruling coalition — belonging to both the PML-N and PPP — were on the receiving end of the state’s excesses during their time in opposition. Perhaps they should remember their own experiences, and the commitments their leaders made to upholding the rule of law.
Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

title: The generational bargain
author: none@none.com (Asif Saad)
content:
OVER my working life, I have watched the next generation enter organisations with different expectations. Business leaders today frequently complain that younger employees view careers, loyalty and work differently from earlier generations. That may be so, but we should also ask whether the economic proposition attached to work has changed. For many young people today, the connection between work, progress and economic security is much less certain. Perhaps that is one reason something interesting is happening across very different parts of the world.
In France, Spain, Belgium, and Albania, young people have been prominent in protests around issues pertaining to education, housing, public services, living costs, and austerity. In India, a youth-led protest movement that began around examinations and electoral processes appears to reflect a deeper frustration about jobs, opportunity and institutions. The circumstances are clear­­­ly different, and it would be simplistic to describe this as a single global movement. But perhaps young people in these very different societies are asking versions of the same question. Does the economic system they have inherited still offer them a credible path towards a better life?
For much of the post-World War II period, the bargain was reasonably clear. Get educated, find employment, work hard, buy a home, accumulate some assets, and eventually retire with reasonable security. Each generation could expect to live better than the previous one. But this bargain is beginning to look less certain. When we think about inequality, we normally think about rich and poor, or capital and labour. An important divide nowadays may, instead, be between those who already own assets and those still trying to acquire them.
Property, financial assets, pensions, family bu­­si­­nesses, and inherited wealth all create advantages that compound over time. The child of a fa­­m­­ily that already owns capital begins adult life in a fundamentally different position from someone who depends entirely on wages. This does not mean that wealth accumulated legitimately is wrong. Saving, investment, entrepreneurship, and risk-taking remain essential to economic progress. The more difficult question is what happens when advantage becomes self-perpetuating.
Across very different societies, young people are asking whether the economic system still offers them a credible stake in the future.
Europe faces another dimension of this problem. Young workers are entering economies with expensive housing, strained public services, and ageing populations. At the same time, they are being asked to finance pension and welfare systems created under very different demographic conditions. The current protests across Europe differ in their immediate causes, but education, housing, public services, and living costs repeatedly appear among the grievances.
India presents almost the opposite demogra­phic picture, yet the underlying anxiety can be surprisingly similar. Its economy has continued to grow rapidly, but growth alone does not guarantee the quantity and quality of employment expected by an increasingly educated young population. Recent protests have had specific institutional triggers, but concern about opportunity and the credibility of the pathway from education to employment sits in the background.
How are young people everywhere reacting to the underlying issues? Some respond by demanding greater redistribution and stronger public services. Others move towards nationalist or populist politics. Others simply lose confidence in established institutions. 
Governments often point to achievements in economic growth, employment or falling inflation and struggle to understand why dissatisfaction remains so intense. But young people may be asking a different question. They are not simply asking whether the economy is growing. They are asking whether they can build a secure life within it. This may also explain why younger employees sometimes seem less attached to careers and organisations than earlier generations were. A young person may have a respectable income but still be unable to buy a home, accumulate meaningful assets, or feel confident about retirement. Economically, such a person may be classified as middle class. In lived experience, they may feel permanently insecure.
An emerging divide, therefore, may not simply be between the rich and poor. It is between those who already possess economic security and those still trying to acquire it. That is a more difficult problem for governments, because it cannot be solved simply by increasing GDP.
This is where Pakistan should pay attention. We always describe our young population as a demographic dividend. But demographics do not create dividends by themselves. Young people become an economic asset only when an economy can educate them, employ them productively, and give them a reasonable expectation that effort will improve their lives.
What exactly is the bargain we offer a young Pakistani today? Get educated, compete for too few productive jobs, struggle with housing and as­­set prices that have moved well beyond ordinary incomes, enter an economy in which family capital and connections matter enormously, and help support a state carrying large pension and debt obligations accumulated over previous decades.
Economic systems ultimately require legitimacy. People are more willing to accept unequal outcomes when they believe opportunity remains open, effort is rewarded, and their children have a reasonable prospect of advancement. Once that confidence disappears, inequality becomes more than a statistic. It becomes political. For much of the past century, the debate around capitalism has centred on whether markets can generate growth and prosperity. The harder question now is whether the prosperity they generate continues to offer succeeding generations a meaningful stake in it.
Unless young people can see a credible route from education to work and from work to economic security, the problem will not simply be that they have less than previous generations. It will be that they no longer believe the system gives them a fair chance. And that is what the protests everywhere are beginning to tell us and what business leaders and policymakers at home need to pay attention to. 
The writer advises boards and CEOs on strategy, leadership and organisational transformation.

title: Toll on trade
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
A YEAR after Islamabad severed commercial ties with Kabul over security concerns, the border trade disruption is taking a growing toll on KP, where livelihoods, businesses, farm markets, and a large number of workers depend on cross-border commerce. Bilateral trade has fallen by more than 72pc, from $1.3bn in FY25 to $358m in FY26 — which means fewer customers for local shops, lower earnings for farmers, idle trucks, and lost jobs. KP was already struggling to attract investment and create work amid rising terrorism; the loss of an established market makes recovery harder. The damage is not confined to the province. Farmers and factories in Punjab and Sindh, too, have been hit, and Pakistan’s exports to Central Asia have been badly disrupted.
Afghanistan has long been KP’s natural outlet because of its proximity and the long-standing commercial and tribal networks. Traders built their businesses around moving food, cement, pharmaceuticals, and other goods across the border. Medical tourism, hotels, and other services catering to Afghan visitors are suffering as well. When crossings shut, traders cannot send their goods to distant markets without facing higher costs, finding new buyers, and adapting to unfamiliar commercial conditions. In fact, most services cannot be shifted at all. Rerouting shipments is not an easy fix. Pakistan’s shortest land routes to Central Asia run through Afghanistan. Alternatives mean longer distances, higher freight costs, and thinner margins. Small enterprises with little financial cushion are the most exposed to prolonged border trade closures. KP needs expanding markets and productive investment to employ a growing workforce; it cannot afford to lose existing ones before alternatives are in place. Islamabad has valid security concerns — the Taliban must prevent Afghan territory from being used for attacks on Pakistan. But border closures also hurt citizens on both sides, who have nothing to do with Kabul’s policies. Islamabad must find the right balance between its security priorities and the economic strain on KP’s residents. Sustained efforts to obtain genuine security assurances from Kabul and carefully monitored arrangements for legitimate trade may offer a way to protect both. It should also assess the losses of traders, transporters, and farmers, and help businesses find new markets. The government must protect its people from terrorism without restricting their livelihoods.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: Emergency matters
author: none@none.com (Arifa Noor)
content:
THE new setup in KP is taking shape rapidly and quietly. While everyone seems focused on the collective meltdown in the PTI, the province the party ruled until recently is busy setting up a new structure.
The governor announced his new advisory council within days, while the emergency-stricken districts have been provided with their own administrative machinery. A special emergency has been declared in the former Fata regions as well as Bannu, Lakki Marwat, Tank, and Dera Ismail Khan.
According to the information available in news reports, these regions will now be managed by a new Area Development Secretariat (ADS), which is to be headed by a bureaucrat, Yahya Akhundzada, an additional chief secretary (ACS). It is being reported that he has been given extensive powers akin to those of a cabinet or a provincial government. Along with this, a new council has been formed, consisting of four people from each district to assist him. An additional inspector general (AIG) of police is also part of this council. Most of these members have been selected, with a few refusals; not bad for a week’s worth of work.
At the federal level, a committee headed by Ishaq Dar has been formed to supervise the province. Besides Dar, the committee includes several PML-N stalwarts, mostly from Punjab, such as Rana Sanaullah, Azam Nazeer Tarar, and Attaullah Tarar. However, other members include Amir Muqam from KP and Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui from Karachi.
At times, the plan appears more ambitious than merely addressing terrorism and governance in KP. In the past week, whispers have been heard around Islamabad; well-informed journalists have also appeared on television and suggested that this setup might decide the future of the other provinces as well. If the technocratic cabinets are able to perform well, there is a chance similar setups may be introduced elsewhere. Faisal Vawda, who, too, has much inside news to share, has suggested or hinted at something similar.
This is lent credence by the manner in which the new administration has been installed in KP, where governor’s rule is accompanied by a special setup for the 12 districts; if there were ever to be smaller provinces in the country, these districts could easily take the form of a ‘South Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’ province.
At times, the plan appears more ambitious than merely addressing terrorism and governance in KP.
Be that as it may, all these ambitious plans — if there are any — will have to wait until the wrinkles are ironed out in KP. I say this because, from the outside, there seems to be a lack of clarity at the moment.
There is some confusion about how this new setup will work. After all, not only is there a governor now in charge of the province, but there is also a powerful ADS for southern KP. So, will the ADS report to the governor or directly to the federal government? That is a bit unclear at the moment.
This also raises the question of what the ADS’s relationship will be with the provincial bureaucracy. If the ACS and AIG report directly to Islamabad, will this eliminate the need to work with Peshawar entirely?
Journalists from the province say the ADS and the federal government will handle development and security directly. This is why the ADS, according to one colleague, is even being given its own set of finance and planning officials. These officials will be part of the new secretariat.
But what will happen in matters that do not fall under development and security, such as education and health?
That is why some feel that, for the moment, there may still be a need to coordinate with the provincial bureaucracy and thrash out other issues. And if that is the case, it can cause delays and hurdles. After all, red tape and bureaucratic hurdles are routine in the country, but if, in this case, rules need to be figured out or made anew, the delays might be more severe.
In addition, as mentioned earlier, there is confusion over how many issues in this special region will go directly to the prime minister or the provincial setup/governor before being routed to the prime minister. While journalists from KP feel the prime minister and Islamabad will deal with all matters directly, the ADR spokesman said in a television interview that the prime minister would handle issues in which the governor and his team could not address the needs of the 12 districts.
If the prime minister, or rather the federal government, is to look after every issue, will decision-making power go to the Dar-led committee? It is hard to imagine that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will have the time to look into every matter individually. The prime minister also prefers to manage matters through committees. But how efficient will this prove to be? Of course, the assumption is that decision-making will be quick and efficient because it will take place elsewhere, and the committees we see exist in name only.
No doubt, this is always a possibility, but how many governance issues can be managed this way? Development and security decisions can perhaps be handled in this manner, but will there be no other issues? Though one should remain optimistic, I suppose.
However, let me venture to say that if this new technocratic setup proves to be successful and efficient, it might just end up increasing centralisation of decision-making, which is far removed from the idea of local government and service delivery at the people’s doorstep. For residents of the 12 districts, Islamabad and cities beyond are much farther away than Peshawar.
The writer is a journalist.

title: Trump & Pakistan
author: none@none.com (Touqir Hussain)
content:
WRITING about Pakistan-US ties is like penning literary criticism of a Shakespearean play. One constantly reinterprets and looks for new answers to old questions. How does one evaluate Pak-US ties under President Donald Trump? Do Trump’s extravagant compliments to Pakistan’s leadership reflect happy relations between the two countries? The short answer is no. American leaders routinely indulge in hyperbole. Add to it the sales pitch of a marketing ‘genius’, and you get Trump’s effusive but effervescent compliments.
Compared to Joe Biden’s time, US-Pakistan ties have no doubt been elevated, but not upgraded. The uptick stems from more than Trump’s bonhomie with Pakistan’s leadership. The relationship is largely a function of his experimental foreign policy. He is reassessing America’s China policy and relations with Russia, rebalancing ties with traditional allies and partners — to America’s advantage — and deprioritising, though not abandoning, the traditional foreign policy establishment’s overweening ambitions to maintain US global primacy. The emphasis is on unilateralism, the naked use of military power, and economic warfare.
This foreign policy stems from his whims, with his politics oriented towards the MAGA movement and the rich class, especially tech billionaires; tariffs used as leverage not only for trade but also for geopolitical gain; and a search for greater market share for America, as well as potential investment and business deals with China and Russia. Pakistan has been an incidental beneficiary of Trump’s policies, good or bad. It has again tried to play its historical role of rescuer in America’s adventures. It has gained by dramatically enhancing its diplomatic profile in the Middle East and its image in America. Washington appears to appreciate the need to maintain Pakistan’s defence capability for regional stability, especially in South Asia, and to use it as leverage against India.
Pakistan, a populous country and a nuclear power, occupies an important geostrategic position between the subcontinent, Iran, Arabia, Central Asia, Russia, and China. Its strength is an asset, and its weakness a liability. One makes it a useful partner; the other makes it hard to ignore, much less alienate. Washington wants to contain China’s political and economic profile in Pakistan. Alienating it would shut the door on all US influence.
The US benefits from a tangible relationship with Pakistan.
America benefits from a tangible relationship with Pakistan in various areas of cooperation. The Trump administration approved a $686 million upgrade and sustainment package for Pakistan’s F-16 fleet. Separately, a $488m foreign military sales contract was awarded to Northrop Grumman for APG-66 and APG-68 radar engineering and technical support, covering 21 countries, including Pakistan. Pak-US cooperation is also developing in the economic area, mainly in energy, IT, crypto, agriculture, renewable energy, and critical minerals, where Pakistan is drawing attention as a significant source. America is also the top destination for Pakistan’s exports. The US needs Pakistan’s cooperation to act against transnational terrorists who endanger regional, American, and global security. Counterterrorism cooperation thus continues. Lastly, Washington has always been concerned about a Pakistan-India conflict and will continue to play a crisis management role.
Behind the veneer of Trump’s rhetoric and personalised foreign policy, however, traditional foreign policy seems to be at work, led by China hawk and pro-India Secretary of Sta­te Marco Rubio, which may be circumscribing Pak-US ties. Oth­erwise, how do we explain that neither he, nor the deputy secreta­­ry, nor an under-secretary of state has visited Pakistan? There’s no semblance of a strategic relationship, despite Rubio’s lip service to the idea.
So, is Trump pursuing a dual-track policy, especially regarding the China policy and its derivative India policy, that influences the administration’s approach to Pakistan? Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hinted at the ‘real’ China policy when he said in an interview that the relationship with China poses an unprecedented national security challenge. “China is … the biggest economic threat, and they’re the biggest military threat,” he said.
The reality is that Trump hasn’t done anything extraordinary for Pakistan that we might fear losing. Much of his freelance foreign policy will likely depart with him, but the impact on Pak-US ties might be minimal. US-Israeli wars in the Middle East have dented America’s standing in the region, providing a fresh rationale for continued engagement with Pakistan in the post-Trump world.
Bottom line: The relationship with the US is necessary but not indispensable. We should keep it that way to safeguard our strategic autonomy. 
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: Burnt bridges
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
A WEEK after the federal government imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP, PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari invited the opposition to engage ‘positively’ with the centre, saying this could lead to their reversal. Mr Bhutto-Zardari, addressing reporters at a Sunday memorial for the 2007 Karsaz attack on his late mother Benazir Bhutto’s homecoming procession, spoke about the need for a national effort to address the growing economic crisis, resurgent terrorism, and Pakistan’s increasingly dysfunctional electoral system. But his offer, however well-meaning, stands little chance of leading to a political breakthrough in the current climate. Without concrete confidence-building measures initiated by the ruling parties, the opposition is unlikely to put much faith in mere assurances, given that the centre has crossed a major political red line by deposing an elected provincial government and supplanting it with a setup handpicked by Islamabad.
Mr Bhutto-Zardari seemed to be missing the point when he called the ‘non-functional’ KP chief minister a “coward” who was “not ready to defend his own land”. Whatever his failings, the people of KP had elected him, and the remedy lay with them, not with Islamabad. By forcing him aside, the centre has signalled that it does not need public consensus to do as it pleases. The centre’s dispute with KP, after all, was not about whether terrorism needed confronting, but how. KP had resisted the centre’s approach to fighting terrorism, and the resulting stand-off had stymied any progress. In dismissing the provincial government, the centre had signalled that security policies would be prescribed for the province rather than derived in consultation with it. That bridge has already been burnt.
It is commendable that the PPP chairperson is at least talking about a path back to normalcy, but the PPP is a partner in the very government that imposed governor’s rule. If it wants the decision reversed, it should convince its ally in Islamabad, not ask the opposition to be ‘positive’. It is hoped that the PML-N will also reconsider its position. The latter party would do well to recall that, in 2009, when its government in Punjab was dismissed and governor’s rule imposed, it had itself joined a ‘long march’ on Islamabad to press its demands. It is unbecoming of that party to have denied its opponents the same right to protest now, when it is in power. It will not be easy to build bridges with the opposition, but the PML-N, more than any other party, has the power to concede some ground to show goodwill. It should take up the National Assembly opposition leader on his offer to engage the jailed PTI chief, and facilitate that effort if it is serious about national reconciliation and a unified response to Pakistan’s crises.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: The data centre and water question
author: none@none.com (Shahzaib Saqib WarraichMuhammad Hassan Dajana)
content:
AS plans for large data centres take shape in Pakistan, the debate has centred on jobs and investment, while a more basic concern has received little attention: water. Why would a data centre compete for water? Computing generates heat, and evaporating water is one of the most cost-effective ways to remove it. By 2030, the United Nations University projects that data centres globally will use nearly triple the combined electricity usage of Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nigeria, with an associated water footprint equal to the basic domestic needs of 1.3 billion people. In Pakistan, the per capita water availability had plummeted from 5,600 cubic metres in 1947 to roughly 930 by 2023.
Some weeks ago, we argued in these pages for bringing compute to where Pakistan’s surplus electricity sits, thereby monetising capacity that consumers already pay for. Water is integral to this equation, and a deeper analysis is warranted, which we aim to provide here.
How data centres keep cool: Data centres are usually cooled through open evaporative systems, which results in most of the water being lost to the atmosphere. However, these systems are comparatively cost-effective and relatively energy-efficient. Other options include closed-loop systems that recirculate water or a coolant through sealed pipes, which can cut freshwater use by up to 70 per cent; and direct-to-chip and immersion cooling, which bring liquid straight to the processor. Additionally, dry cooling uses almost no water but, by Google’s own estimate, about 10pc more energy. So there is a trade-off in cost and energy, but for a country like ours that already pays for idle generation, it is a strategic investment choice.
Running the numbers: A 2016 US Department of Energy study puts average on-site data centre water use at 1.8 litres per kWh. At that rate, a 1 GW campus running continuously would consume about 16 million cubic metres a year, roughly 0.01pc of the 175 billion cubic metres the Indus supplies annually. Sky47’s 8.5MW Karakoram-01 would, based on these estimates, use around 134,000 cubic metres a year. Even accounting for Pakistan’s hotter temperatures, these figures remain marginal. Hence, nationally, data centres are not Pakistan’s water problem.
Thirsty infrastructure is workable when siting follows the water.
However, locally they can be. A 1 GW campus would draw about 10 million gallons a day from a single source, the same volume that Karachi’s new Rs14bn Dumlottee pipeline will add for the Defence and Clifton areas, in a city receiving 550-650 million gallons daily against a demand of around 1,200 million gallons. The burden falls on the nearest communities.
Pakistan has faced this question of siting before with its nuclear power plants. Reactors with cooling towers consume about 2.5 litres per kWh, according to a 2012 review by the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory. At 6,755 GWh generated by Karachi’s K-3 unit in 2024, by the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission’s count, that’s about 17 million cubic metres a year, or about 12 million gallons a day, more than a 1 GW data centre campus. Pakistan avoided that burden through siting: K-2 and K-3 sit on the coast and cool with seawater, while Chashma draws on the Chashma-Jhelum link canal. Thirsty infrastructure is workable when siting follows the water.
The problem at the foundation: Pakistan’s water crisis lies elsewhere. More than 93pc of its water goes to agriculture, and over 60pc of that is lost in conveyance and application. Four crops (rice, wheat, sugarcane, and cotton) consume over 80pc of water resources yet contribute about 5pc of GDP; Pakistan generates just $1.4 of GDP per cubic metre withdrawn, the eighth-lowest in the world. The parallel with power is striking: consumers pay for electricity that never reaches them, and the country withdraws water that never reaches a crop.
The way forward: Three interventions follow:
1) Immediate: make water a licensing condition, with energy-compute zones mandating closed-loop or dry cooling, public reporting of water use, and siting away from stressed aquifers. Dubai has promoted recycled water in district cooling since 2008, and Qatar has long incentivised non-potable cooling.
2) Short-term: cool with wastewater. Pakistan treats barely 1pc of its collected wastewater. Meanwhile, Chennai’s tertiary treatment plants are designed to recycle a fifth of the city’s sewage for industry, and Amazon, which air-cools its Indian data centres, will use treated sewage in upcoming facilities in Mumbai and Hyderabad. Operators could co-finance similar plants in Karachi and Lahore.
3) Long-term: reform agricultural water use. Punjab’s World Bank-backed irrigation programme improved over 15,000 watercourses while promoting drip irrigation and laser-levelling. Scaling it nationally and shifting acreage from rice and sugarcane towards pulses, vegetables, and sunflower would save water and cut edible oil imports. Saving just 1pc of the Indus water used for irrigation would supply a 1 GW campus for a century.
Weighing both sides: Both sides of this debate hold part of the truth. Critics are right that a poorly sited data centre can strain a community; advocates are right that the sector will not exhaust a country. Pakistan has missed too many economic waves to let a misframed debate cost it this one. The power and water are there to support the data centre industry. What remains is the discipline to manage matters both wisely and efficiently. 
The writers are Fulbright scholars.

title: Climate exodus
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
SOUTH Asia may see a vast movement of people as climate change makes parts of the region harder to live in. According to the International Organisation for Migration, as many as 40.5m people could be forced to move by 2050. The warning deserves attention for what such displacement could mean for a region already struggling with poverty, overcrowded cities, unemployment, and competition for resources. From the sinking coastlines of Bangladesh to the drought-hit districts of Pakistan, climate pressures are threatening millions of livelihoods. But it is not just the communities directly affected that will feel the impact. As farmers abandon unproductive land and families leave disaster-prone areas, towns and cities will have to accommodate growing populations. Competition for housing, employment, water and public services could make life harder for poorer communities and generate social tensions. Countries with limited resources may struggle to provide for both established residents and newcomers. The danger is particularly acute in South Asia, where weak regional cooperation could hinder a coordinated response. Climate displacement could then become another source of instability unless governments prepare for it together.
The warning raises questions about how Pakistan intends to accommodate people whose homes and livelihoods become impossible to sustain. Our urban centres already struggle with inadequate housing, sanitation, transport, and job opportunities. An influx of climate-displaced families could deepen these problems. Yet migration need not mean destitution. As the IOM chief has pointed out, moving can itself be a means of adapting to climate change. Pakistan must, therefore, recognise climate mobility as a permanent consideration in development planning. Provincial and local governments need reliable information about communities likely to leave, destinations likely to receive them, and services required to support their transition. Land-use policies, affordable housing, vocational training, and access to schools and healthcare must reflect changing population patterns. Equally important is protecting the rights of displaced families, who should not lose access to documentation, education or public assistance simply because they have moved. Regional cooperation on forecasting, disaster preparedness and population movements could help countries anticipate shared pressures. The challenge is to ensure that people forced to move by climate change can rebuild their lives.
Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

title: Devolution deficit
author: none@none.com (Aisha Khan)
content:
PAKISTAN’S climate challenge is a test of whether a decentralised but politically fragmented federation can govern collective risks. Climate-induced disasters do not stop at provincial boundaries. Yet institutions responsible for responding remain divided by federal-provincial tensions and ethnic and regional competition within provinces. The 18th Amendment is often portrayed as a source of fragmentation. That interpretation is incomplete. The amendment was primarily a response to excessive centralisation and provincial grievances. Its paradox is that, while it reduced vertical tensions between the centre and provinces, it did not ensure that power would travel further downward to districts and communities. 
The 18th Amendment addressed the imbalance by abolishing the Concurrent Legislative List. The seventh NFC Award raised the provincial share of the divisible pool from 45 to 57.5 per cent. The difficulty emerged at the next level. Provincial autonomy did not automatically produce meaningful local autonomy. Article 140A requires provinces to establish local governments (LGs) and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility and authority to elected representatives. In practice provincial political elites have often retained control over resources and decision-making. Authority has moved away from the centre without necessarily moving close enough to citizens, who experience climate risks most directly.
This matters because climate governance depends on coordination at multiple levels that requires national forecasting and financing, provincial planning and district-level preparedness. Without empowered local institutions, climate policy remains concentrated in provincial capitals, where political priorities may compete and implementation capacity is weakest at the point of delivery.
Intra-provincial tensions add another layer of difficulty. In Sindh, concentration of political and administrative authority in Karachi and the PPP’s dominance have contributed to a sharp urban-rural divide. In Punjab, perceptions of financial and administrative dominance by Lahore have sustained grievances in the Seraiki belt with demands for a separate south Punjab province. In KP, the renaming of the province as part of the 18th Amendment settlement generated resistance in the Hindko-speaking Hazara region and renewed demands for a separate province. These conflicts shape who controls development funds, infrastructure, public services and political representation — all central to climate resilience.
Climate change demands more than a simple division of federal powers.
The centre also faces constraints. Federal policymakers have argued that the post-18th Amendment fiscal settlement limits resources available for national responsibilities. Provinces, in turn, regard attempts to dilute their fiscal or legislative autonomy as a threat to constitutional guarantees. Pakistan needs national standards, shared data, coordinated disaster response, climate finance, international reporting and the capacity to meet commitments under global climate agreements. Provinces need meaningful authority over sectors affecting adaptation and resilience.
Climate change, therefore, exposes the limits of treating federalism as a simple division of powers. Pakistan requires a system in which autonomy and coordination reinforce each other. The 18th Amendment should not be blamed for ethnic polarisation; rather, its unfinished devolution agenda should be addressed. Provincial governments need to make Article 140A meaningful by transferring predictable finances, administrative authority, and decision-making powers to elected LGs. Federal and provincial institutions also need permanent mechanisms for joint climate pl­­anning, shared infor­mation, di­­saster prepare­dness, and fi­­n­a­ncing, while en­­­-suring that vulnerable regions and communities have a genuine voice.
The 18th Am­­endment is not the primary driver of ethnic divisions. However, the failure of regional ruling parties to pass these fruits down via local body governance has transformed old centre-province animosities into localised, intra-provincial ethnic fracturing. 
The root causes of the recent developments in KP can partly be linked to 16 years of uneven development exacerbated by political miscalculations and exploited by vested interest groups. This trend can lead to deeper alienation without local body governance. 
The real challenge is to prevent decentralisation from ending at provincial capitals. Climate adaptation cannot remain trapped in federal-provincial bargaining or intra-provincial ethnic competition. A resilient federation must combine autonomy with empowered LGs, cooperation and equitable access to climate resources for all its citizens. 
The writer is a climate policy analyst.

title: Ethiopian sea fever
author: none@none.com (Zarrar Khuhro)
content:
WITH attention sharply focused on Iran and the Saudi-Ansarullah conflict, you may be forgiven for not noticing that the East African nation of Eritrea has invaded its much larger neighbour Ethiopia. On the face of it, this is insane: Ethiopia’s population is at least 30 times that of its smaller neighbour and its GDP of $140 billion dwarfs Eritrea’s modest $2bn. In military terms, while Eritrea — thanks to its national service policy — fields a large army consisting of some 350,000 active duty soldiers and approximately 650,000 reservists, these are largely poorly armed, equipped and trained and heavily outgunned by Ethiopia, which has greatly modernised its military in recent years.
Nevertheless, Eritrean forces entered Ethiopian territory in late September this year, sparking clashes with the Ethiopian army. Is Eritrea insane for taking on its much larger neighbour? Not quite. The incursion comes at a time when Ethiopia is facing an alliance of rebels that have banded together with the aim of toppling Ethiopian president Abiy Ahmed’s government. The alliance unites seven groups including the Oromo Liberation army, the Fano militia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front. The TPLF have an interesting history here; staging repeated rebellions against Ethiopian rule, the Tigrayan-led Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front actually held power in Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 when they were sidelined by the current Ethiopian leadership leading to what is known as the Tigray war of 2020-2022.
Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea are even more contentious: when Eritrea became independent in 1993 following a brutal 30-year conflict, it effectively cut off Ethiopia’s access to the Red Sea, something that Abiy Ahmed wants to rectify. Ethiopia and Eritrea did have a brief rapprochement during the Tigray war, when they joined forces against the TPLF. Yes, the same TPLF that Eritrea is now supporting against Ethiopia; another object lesson that while alliances are temporary, interests are permanent.
Eritrea has reason to believe that if Ethiopia manages to subdue the rebels, a victorious Ethiopian army will march into Eritrea and wrest access to the Red Sea, something that Abiy deems as ‘inevitable’ and an ‘existential’ need for his country. He’s not wrong; the most populous landlocked country in the world, Ethiopia is forced to rely on the Addis-Djibouti corridor for 95 per cent of its export-import trade and has to pay close to $2bn annually in transit and port fees.
Is Eritrea insane for taking on its much larger neighbour?
But its rush to the Red Sea is setting off alarm bells among coastal states, notably Somalia, which is livid at Abiy’s outreach to the breakaway so-called Republic of Somaliland, that has also pledged its full support to Ethiopia’s quest for the Red Sea and is considering leasing 19 kilometres to Ethiopia. It’s worth noting that the only country to have formally recognised Somaliland is Israel, and Somaliland also has very close relations with Israel’s chief Arab ally, the UAE.
Why is this important? Because while Saudi Arabia and Turkiye currently have good relations with Ethiopia, neither would be delighted to have Ethiopia formally become a littoral state of the Red Sea, and in Turkiye’s case, certainly not at the cost of Somalia, with which Turkiye has massively expanded its relations, encompassing both the military and economic spheres. For the embattled Saudis, having a state closely allied to Israel and the UAE expand its power in this manner may have negative long-term consequences. 
But while these are somewhat distant concerns, the expanding conflict in East Africa is certainly drawing Egypt’s attention. Why? Because Egypt, as Herodotus wrote in the 5th century BC, is “a gift of the Nile”, a saying that is as true today as it was then, and Ethio­pia’s plan to build the ‘Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam’ on the headwaters of the Nile poses an existential threat to Egypt.
Thus, it is in Egypt’s interests to curtail Ethiopian power as much as possible by supporting Eritrea. And then there’s Sudan, where Ethiopia is accused not only of allowing the use of its territory for arms shipments from the UAE to the rebel RSF in Sudan, but also (along with the UAE) by the Sudanese army of carrying out drone strikes on Sudanese soil. Moreover, a recent investigation by Reuters claims to have uncovered a training camp for the Rapid Support Forces in Western Ethiopia. To be fair, Ethiopia’s actions are also dictated by its financial dependence on the UAE (the RSF’s chief backer) and its fears that a victory of the Sudanese army — relations between the two have never been good — will result in a strategic encirclement of Ethiopia. And so, we see that, once again, fear and financial imperatives are stoking another conflict that will not stay confined to one region. 
The writer is a journalist.

title: Persisting fault lines
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
HISTORY, it has famously been said, repeats itself first as tragedy and then as farce. Today, it is repeating itself in Pakistan as both tragedy and farce. Recent events have deepened some of the country’s overlapping fault lines — enduring features that have shaped its political landscape for decades. Together they have contributed to its chronic instability and impeded its progress. It has meant the absence of a calm and predictable environment in which to meet the country’s growing challenges. The country seems caught in a time warp with a power elite ensuring it cannot escape its past.  
Four fault lines (there are others too) are laid bare by recent political developments: unceasing confrontation between the government and opposition; centre-province conflict resulting in dismissal of elected provincial governments; parliament’s marginal role in the political system; and weak institutions whose evolution is stymied or independence eroded by predatory ruling elites. 
The ongoing confrontation between the PML-N-led government and PTI may have novel aspects but it reflects a long-standing fault line in the country’s divisive politics. Government-opposition conflicts have been endemic in Pakistan’s history, with political behaviour driven by the ethic of war rather than competition. Political leaders and parties have viewed opponents as enemies to be eliminated from the political arena in a terminal conflict, not rivals to compete with, much less accommodated. Branding opponents as disloyal to the country is a well-worn, unseemly tradition. This is evident today by the disingenuous narrative peddled by federal ministers that the ousted KP government was aligned with terrorist organisations. 
A culture of compromise, tolerance, and restraint never took root leaving ruling and opposition parties perpetually at loggerheads. This, in turn, opened the door to both direct and indirect interventions by the military, which could always count on support from one political party or another to oust governments and expand its power. Divide and rule strategies pursued by the establishment also fuelled political conflict. 
Some enduring aspects of the political landscape are holding Pakistan back.
There were rare moments of political consensus as for example when the 1973 Constitution was adopted, Charter of Democracy agreed (but never implemented) between Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif in 2006 and in more recent years, the unanimous passage of the 18th Constitutional Amendment in 2010. Beyond these and some other exceptions, the tradition of intolerance and authoritarian behaviour has persisted.
Opposition parties have rarely accepted the legitimacy of governments while governments refused to recognise opposition as a legitimate activity fundamental to democracy. The underlying reason has usually been disputed elections. Pakistan’s history is replete with losing sides contesting results and alleging ballot fraud, often for good reason. This happened most recently in the 2024 election which, despite its controversial nature, still saw PTI winning a plurality in the national legislature. It was blocked from forming the federal government by an alliance between its opponents and the establishment. Its uncompromising conduct today stems from what it sees as a stolen election and political manoeuvring to keep it out of power. 
While linked to government-opposition conflict, the second fault line is distinct: troubled relations and friction between the centre and provinces, which have punctuated the country’s history and weakened federalism. Intolerance of opposition-controlled provincial governments by parties governing at the centre became a common feature from the very inception of Pakistan. Just seven days after independence, the NWFP government was deposed, setting an unfortunate precedent. Thereafter, every province saw elected governments replaced by governor’s rule at some time or another, undermining the federation and testing the country’s unity. The consequences of intolerance of rivals together with the establishment’s efforts to centralise power and failure to make the federal arrangement work, were writ large in the rise of the Bengali nationalist movement that culminated in the break-up of Pakistan in 1971.
But no lesson was learnt and the fault line endured. Fast forward to the 1990s when the regionalised nature of election outcomes meant that parties forming governments at the federal level were often different from those that constituted provincial governments. This should have urged efforts to establish smooth and cooperative centre-province relations. But that did not happen. The notion that reciprocal obligations between the centre and provinces are more than a constitutional precept and actually have to be fulfilled by both sides still finds few takers.
A third fault line relates to parliament’s weakness and its inability to play its fundamental role of exercising oversight of executive actions and hold governments to account. Successive governments have viewed parliament principally as a means to maintain themselves in power rather than a forum to initiate and debate laws and policy. The preferred mode of legislating has often been through ordinance or using a brute majority to rush through laws without deliberation. This reduced parliament to little more than a rubber stamp. The most recent examples are the 26th and 27th Constitutional amendments that were steamrolled through parliament in 2024 and 2025 without real debate and without even sharing their texts with members before moving them. There was virtually no debate when the two chambers recently endorsed the imposition of emergency in KP. Few if any governments encouraged parliament to play an active legislative and deliberative role. Instead, they preferred the legislature to be a passive body. This remains the case.  
Even ruling parties with handsome majorities failed to recognise parliament’s utility as a forum to ventilate, change and share opinion. Whether this reflects lack of confidence in their backbenchers or poor understanding of how parliament should function, the outcome is marginalisation of the legislature’s role. This denudes the political system of democratic accountability.
The fourth fault line — weak institutions — is no less consequential. It is rooted in a political culture that has privileged personalities over institutions, and in a ruling elite that has little appetite for strong institutions because they impose checks and balances and place limits on power. Nothing illustrates this better than the judiciary. Its independence has been steadily eroded over the years by both civilian and military governments. The recent constitutional amendments have taken this further, making the superior judiciary subservient to the executive.
Political fault lines are not cast in stone. Their persistence doesn’t mean they cannot be overcome especially when their impact on the country is so damaging. But it requires bold, visionary leadership to break from the past. 
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

title: Settler terrorism
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
ISRAEL’S genocidal violence in occupied Gaza has understandably captured the world’s attention. Yet another pernicious campaign, overseen by the Zionist state, is underway in the West Bank, under the guise of illegal settlements — what the Palestinian Authority accurately terms ‘settler terrorism’. The menace of unlawful Israeli settlements in the occupied territories came up during a recent UN Security Council debate, with states calling for a halt to these blatantly illegal outposts. The Pakistani delegate pointed out that settlements threaten the “viability of a future Palestinian state”, while the French representative said they fuel “instability”. Illegal settlements have grown rapidly over the last few years; there are over 500 such unlawful communities, serving as home to hundreds of thousands of people comprising some of the most radical and violent members of Israel’s Jewish population. Violence against native Palestinians is commonplace, as settlers carry out a campaign of ethnic cleansing and land grabs, blessed by the Zionist regime. As a senior UN official observed, “the West Bank is at the breaking point”, adding that settler violence had reached “unprecedented levels”.
The horrific violence in Gaza, and the ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, have effectively buried the two-state solution. Israel has shown no intentions of honouring the so-called peace process. As the Palestinian delegate to the UNSC debate asked: “How can Israeli militarism be justified while Palestinian pacifism is demanded?” Unless this double standard is addressed by the global community, a just resolution of the Palestine question is impossible. The remedy is seemingly clear; Israel must end the bloodbath in all the occupied territories, immediately halt and dismantle all illegal settlements, and commit itself to the two-state idea. But the international community will be hard-pressed to find any mainstream Israeli leader — from the nominal left to the hard right — who can commit to these principles.

title: State of denial
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
AS reports continue to do the rounds of possible Russian mediation to resolve the differences between Pakistan and Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, the Foreign Office has underscored that successful dialogue requires commitment from Kabul to end cross-border terrorism.
This demand is neither new nor unreasonable; it highlights the point that talks and support for anti-Pakistan terrorist groups cannot go hand in hand. On Friday, the FO said that while it was not aware of any formal Russian mediation initiative, Pakistan was open to engagement that produced tangible results. Representatives of Pakistan and the Taliban regime were both in Russia earlier this month as part of the Moscow Format regional consultations. A joint communique could not be issued at the conclave due to frosty Islamabad-Kabul ties, specifically because the Taliban objected to including any references to terrorism in Afghanistan. Russia had offered its good offices to resolve the impasse, if both sides required its help.
The official Taliban position amounts to a state of denial: it is hardly a secret that some of the world’s most dangerous terrorist groups find shelter in Afghanistan. Therefore, the Kabul regime’s denials hold no water. Many other third parties — Qatar, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, and China — have tried to mediate between Pakistan and Afghanistan, with varying degrees of success. Russia is the only state that recognises the Taliban regime. Perhaps Moscow can be engaged by Pakistan and Afghanistan to try and give the peace process another chance.
Pakistan and Afghanistan share borders and linguistic and cultural links. Good relations are essential, even though bilateral relations have remained largely strained over the past several decades. However, the biggest obstacle to long-term peace is the Taliban’s sheltering of terrorist groups. Pakistan desires peace, but for talks to succeed, Kabul must offer visible CBMs, such as an end to cross-border terrorism. As the FO has said, a “verifiable mechanism” that ensures an end to anti-Pakistan terrorism emanating from Afghanistan can lead the way to peace. Kabul’s claims that it is not hosting violent groups are of little value.
Action against such groups is required, not hollow refutations. Moreover, regional states must realise that today it is Pakistan that is battling terrorist groups in Afghanistan. Tomorrow, similar violent actors based in that country can destabilise other regional states. Russia itself has been targeted by IS-K terrorism. The group finds a home in Afghanistan, even though it is at daggers drawn with the Taliban. If the Taliban regime commits to preventing groups based on its soil from attacking neighbouring states, the process of normalisation and regional integration of Afghanistan can begin.
Published in Dawn, October 18th, 2026

title: Safe spaces for women
author: none@none.com (Zeba Sathar)
content:
THE Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010, was an important response to problems that directly affect women. It enabled the ombudsman to hear cases, many of which were resolved in women’s favour. A recent judgement has now eliminated an avenue that many women used to report harassment. The Federal Constitutional Court’s ruling, which narrows the interpretation of harassment, is a setback for women’s space in public life.
Unfortunately, it appears to show that a major state institution is prepared to restrict rather than expand women’s safety at work. From birth to death, women and girls in Pakistan face limits on where they can go freely, where they may go only under certain conditions, and where they cannot go at all. Visitors to Pakistan often notice their limited visibility as one of the first features of public life. This absence should not be dismissed as cultural; it largely reflects structural factors.
Restrictions on mobility — driven mainly by concerns about safety — help explain poor educational outcomes for girls, physical inactivity during adolescence, and their alarmingly low participation in the labour force as adults. The lack of safety outside the home is among the most frequently cited reasons for not sending girls to school, alongside poverty and families’ inability to afford schooling. The problem is intensified by the limited availability of girls’ schools in many parts of Pakistan.
Undoubtedly, the shortage of schools and female teachers, together with poor learning quality, creates major barriers. Millions of girls live in districts where the nearest public school is more than an hour away and therefore out of practical reach. These supply-side failures prevent many girls from even imagining that they could enter a classroom. Perceived danger reinforces the barrier at home: some girls never enrol, while others drop out at puberty. At the very least, girls who are fortunate enough to live near a school should not be excluded because the journey is unsafe.
Women’s limited ability to work outside the home is probably the most affected by structural factors.
A Population Council and Unicef study, Adolescent Girls’ Voices on Enhancing Their Own Productivity, found that parents were reluctant to send girls to school because of fear of harassment on the way. This fear has been exacerbated by an incredible surge in social media-related harassment and cyberbullying, thanks to the proliferation of mobile phones and other digital devices. Requiring a chaperone or private transport immediately increases the costs of sending girls to school. Not surprisingly, an estimated 8.3 million girls aged 10 to 19 lack official status — they are neither in school, at work, nor married. This large cohort of girls depicts a decade of lost productivity, learning, and, above all, self-esteem.
The state’s role is clear: protect the rights of all its citizens from harassment and unsafe spaces. It must remove these hurdles by providing structural solutions that enable girls to attend and complete school. Harassment laws that create safe routes and workplaces must be seen as educational policy requirements, not peripheral issues.
Women’s limited ability to work outside the home is probably the most affected by structural factors. It is also the most costly in terms of losses to the economy and society. Female labour force participation rates have remained stagnant at around 22 per cent for the last 15 years. When women earn, they tend to spend more proactively, with direct payoffs for children’s education, health, and general welfare. But this will not happen if women feel unprotected at the workplace.
Although women are generally accepted as schoolteachers and in some health professions, attacks on doctors and Lady Health Workers threaten even these spaces — many work mostly out of economic desperation. Employers are reluctant to give women jobs with longer, more secure contracts because of perceived hazards and domestic duties. At the other end of the spectrum, highly educated and affluent women participate in the labour force, cushioned by family support and private transport. The result is some improvement in women’s participation at the top end for highly educated, privileged women and, at the other end, for the truly desperate who must leave home to buy food and ensure their families’ survival, ie, domestic help, cleaners, and informal sector workers who do the most menial work.
Women’s representation in Pakistan’s parliament is the only positive achievement in the SDGs’ gender indicators. Most elected women come from privileged families, but not all, as the pool expands. The trend began with the mandatory party quota for women. Otherwise, trends of an even more male-dominated parliament would have continued. The handful of women lawmakers have made headway in legislating, or at least highlighting, issues important to women and human rights.
Comparable action is required in laws and public policy to expand women’s participation in every public sphere, especially formal employment. Increasing the number of women in decision-making and other critical positions — particularly in the police and judiciary — would make a tangible difference. A 30pc recruitment quota in the formal sector is essential. Greater representation in formal paid work will generate positive spillover effects in other sectors.
It is especially imperative to address the extremely high unemployment rate (24pc) among young women who have completed more than a secondary education. Despite completing higher levels of education, this group is denied opportunities for secure employment. A quota system and positive supportive legislation will directly and positively affect the current generation whom we repeatedly say we care about the most.
Women and girls must have safe passage and be guarded with assurances that harassment is a punishable offence. Recent measures to improve women’s mobility are encouraging, such as pink buses and scooter loans, but they remain too few and too far apart. Above all, there is a need to change mindsets; a public campaign against harassment of women and girls in public spaces must become a priority.
Society must review its standards and morals and move forward, not backwards, in legislation, run bold campaigns, and do whatever it takes to correct this pernicious course of restricting, rather than expanding, the power of women and girls. 
The writer is country adviser to the Population Council.
Published in Dawn, October 18th, 2026

title: Closing the Afghan file
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Amir Rana)
content:
THE civil-military relationship in Pakistan has never been ideal. Despite recent conciliatory efforts and the policy of accommodation adopted by the coalition government, concerns within security-focused circles persist about the handling of several government affairs. For now, though, there is little chance of an escalation in civil-military tensions involving the federal and provincial governments; the last hitch was the PTI government, which was ousted through governor’s rule and emergency. The major allegation against the PTI government has been that it was hesitant to take a clear position against the terrorists, enabling them to expand their influence in parts of the province, especially in the southern districts.
The establishment is sensitive about the narrative, and considers it subversion and part of hybrid warfare; it looks upon any political or ideological support for it as support to the enemy. Terminology describing Taliban-aligned terrorists as ‘Fitna al-Khwarij’ and Baloch insurgents as ‘Fitna al-Hindustan’ reflects the same approach. Everyone is expected to follow this approach; the PTI government’s disagreement on several security-related policies is, therefore, interpreted as an act of subversion. Meanwhile, it is clear how much civilian governments actually contribute to security-related affairs.
The security domain has often caused friction between the establishment and civilian governments; over the decades, the political leadership has learned not to voice disagreement on security-related affairs. ‘Memogate’ was the last such lesson for the PPP; and ‘Dawn leaks’ for Mian Nawaz Sharif; the removal of Imran Khan’s PTI from its provincial seat of power in KP appears to have followed the same pattern. The story is not simply about subversion or disagreement over security policy. There are other relevant aspects that some commentators have pointed out: among them is the fiscal issue which also triggered the call for new provinces and the reversal of the 18th Amendment. Yet another dimension is linked to closing the Afghan file.
Bhutto’s policy was just the lever. It was Zia who turned it into an ideology.
The Afghan policy has shaped Pakistan’s politics for half a century; but now there is a general acceptance, even within security circles, that it has not worked. It is evident that the state is distancing itself from past approaches. In this regard, some intellectuals and commentators have painted militancy as a cultural expression of Pakhtuns, which the local dynamics of the larger Pakhtun society has aggravated. There is no need to deconstruct such a perception, which would be stigmatisation. In effect, applying a sociocultural lens to the issue takes away focus from the main architects of the security and Afghan policy. The previous Afghan policy worked well but had lost its utility in geopolitical contexts. This was the policy crafted by the military dictator Gen Ziaul Haq and his team, and it was more or less functional until the Taliban captured power in Afghanistan in August 2021. Though the Zia file saw a few changes and amendments, the overall framework for dealing with these affairs did not change much.
The Zia file had a few critical components that even allies including Washington, Beijing, Riyadh, and Ankara had concerns about — particularly the reliance on non-state actors. Mian Nawaz Sharif had drawn attention to it but faced the consequences. Many analysts believe that this flawed policy was responsible for spawning the TTP and generating terrorism in KP but official narratives do not link the state of affairs to the policy choices made earlier. 
Establishment circles appear to want a new Afghan policy that best suits their geopolitical and internal security objectives. A complete detachment from the Taliban is part of the new approach, and the Sohail Afridi government was reluctant to adopt it because it would mean a large-scale military operation, displacement, and increased security-related resource allocation — which would also have political consequences. After the removal of his government, the hurdles preventing a new policy have been eliminated; the new set-up now has to deliver, as was expected of the Afridi government. There will be no opportunity any longer to shift the onus of blame onto a political government, despite official narratives distancing the security state from political change in KP.
However, the dimensions of the new Afghan policy remain unclear. For instance, how will the state proceed if the Afghan Taliban agree to detach themselves from the terrorist networks operating against Pakistan from Afghan soil? Still, another argument being promoted is that Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, not Gen Ziaul Haq, was the real architect of Pakistan’s Afghan policy. There is some truth to that. After Sardar Daud’s 1973 coup in Kabul and his revival of the Pakhtunistan issue, the Bhutto government began hosting and training Afghan Islamists, among them men who would later become the commanders of the anti-Soviet jihad. The FC and a small circle of officials ran this as a pressure tool against Kabul. Notably, the province’s first governor after 1973, appointed in 1975, following the ban on the National Awami Party, reflected the same anxieties about Pakhtun nationalism and Afghanistan.
But Bhutto’s policy was just the lever. It was Zia who turned it into an ideology. After the Soviet invasion of 1979, the Afghan question became the organising principle of the state: the jihad, the refugee economy, the madressah network, the doctrine of strategic depth, and an intelligence apparatus that grew more powerful than the elected institutions meant to oversee it. That legacy matters, and it is Zia’s.
Now it is up to the supporters of the PPP how they take the argument, and whether they are ready to carry the entire burden of history on their shoulders; they also face criticism that Benazir Bhutto continued Bhutto’s legacy and allowed Gen Naseerullah Babar to nurture the Taliban in 1994-96, the same general who had crafted the Afghan files for her father. The Taliban generations have caused huge losses to the PPP, including the assassination of Benazir Bhutto herself. 
The writer is a security analyst.
Published in Dawn, October 18th, 2026

title: Moral consensus
author: none@none.com (Naeem Sadiq)
content:
CANADA’S richest province Ontario, with a GDP of a trillion Canadian dollars, purchased a 10-year-old jet costing 28 million Canadian dollars (Rs5.46 billion) for the official use of its premier. Critics quickly dubbed it the “gravy plane”, taunting Doug Ford’s long-standing political rhetoric about eliminating government waste. The premier was quick to take responsibility. He promptly returned the plane. Far away, in a country where 48 per cent of the people fall in the ‘extremely poor’ category, a chief minister acquired a spanking new Gulfstream 500 — twice as expensive as the plane of the Ontarian premier. It was also followed by similar public outrage. The chief minister, however, vowed to continue using the “gravy plane” as her legal right.
On Sept 30, 2026, something seriously went wrong with the execution of Christa Pike at the Maximum Security Prison in Nashville, Tennessee. The two doses of the lethal pentobarbital injection failed to achieve their intended result. Pike did not die. Just two days later, Frank Strada, commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction, resigned on grounds of moral responsibility. Only a few weeks earlier, 14 newborn babies had been burnt to death in a hospital fire in Islamabad. No one resigned. The executive director had to be forced to step down.
Why is it that countries possessing very similar constitutions, parliaments, democracies, and laws end up achieving radically different outcomes? The ones doing poorly can be recognised by a distinct common denominator: a ruling class deeply deficient in character, values, and moral responsibility. Such nations forever remain in search of new laws, new faces, and new messiahs, rather than seeking a new code of conduct for their morally deficient leaders.
Laws devoid of morality find enough loopholes to justify abuse.
For centuries, slavery was legally permitted. Women were legally denied their right to vote and property. Racial segregation and discrimination were once legally enforced. Children working long hours in hazardous jobs was legally permitted. Workers dying or being seriously injured in mines and sewage gutters was treated as the cost of doing business. But all these ‘legally’ sanctioned practices were inherently unjust and morally decadent. It took decades of determined struggle by the abolitionist, women’s rights, civil rights, and labour movements to establish that legality alone could never legitimise practices that violated the fundamental principles of equality, dignity, safety, and justice.
While Pakistani laws adequately address equality, safety, and dignity, the ruling elite has remained resolutely impervious to any of these considerations and continues to rule with remarkable immorality. Governance has become synonymous with self-enrichment, self-projection, and self-indulgence. Questioning the conduct, wastefulness and misuse of state resources is considered unpatriotic. Pakistan thus faces a grave moral and institutional crisis that cannot be resolved by any new sermons, slogans, changes in government, or enactment of new laws. An ecosystem overflowing with laws but devoid of morality will always find enough loopholes and justifications to perpetuate its questionable practices.
Much as the abolition of slavery required society to move beyond what the law permitted, Pakistan needs a moral consensus on rejecting practices that may be legally permissible yet remain immoral, unequal, undignified, unsafe, and irresponsible. A useful starting point would be to recognise that expenditures such as aircraft and bullet-proof vehicles for the luxury and convenience of the ruling elite, even when legally sanctioned, are downright im­­moral, and should be withdrawn. The excessive self-san­­ctioned salaries, perks and privile­ges of judges, parliamentarians, and government offici­als, even when ba­­cked by legal notifications, are im­­­­­-
moral. Billions of rupees spent on self-publicity, ads, billboards, posters and pictures on every imaginable free space, even when approved by a sycophantic finance department, are wasteful and unethical.
Likewise, naming every building, bridge, school, hospital, and ration bag after a serving politician is morally reprehensible. Sending workers into sewage gutters, even when legally practised for 80 years is despicably immoral and needs to be eliminated forthwith. Not to mention that pathological addiction of borrowing and begging from foreign donors and friendly countries, even when endorsed by law, is demeaning and immoral.
Pakistan must pause, introspect and agree on how to weed out immorality amongst leaders. An agenda for moral reforms that binds the rulers to higher standards of conduct may be far more consequential than a new or recycled set of laws and leaders.
The writer is an industrial engineer and a volunteer social activist.

title: Export imperative
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE government’s efforts to boost Pakistan’s external sector through diversified financing, higher foreign exchange reserves, and improved access to international capital markets are welcome. After years of recurring balance-of-payment crises, the country needs a more reliable strategy to meet its foreign currency obligations. But can Pakistan achieve lasting stability without substantially increasing its capacity to earn foreign exchange? At a meeting with the US Treasury under-secretary in Bangkok, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb discussed the country’s economic outlook, reform agenda, and external financing strategy. In recent months, Pakistan’s access to international capital markets has significantly increased as reflected by the Panda and Eurobond issues this year. But improved access to international debt markets should not be confused with the capacity to generate foreign exchange through exports and FDI.
Diversifying creditors and financing channels can reduce reliance on individual lenders but cannot remove repayment obligations. The government’s stress on export-led growth, IT exports, and competitiveness is, therefore, welcome. The challenge is to translate these ambitions into sustained results. Foreign exchange reserves provide a useful buffer, while fiscal discipline has helped restore confidence. However, reserves can be drawn down by debt repayments, energy imports, and capital outflows. Primary budget surpluses also exclude interest payments, which consume a substantial share of public revenue. Both achievements matter, but neither substitutes for stronger export earnings. Geopolitical tensions and volatile energy prices further complicate matters. Pakistan cannot build a durable external position through periodic bond issues, bilateral support, and rollover of obligations. Ultimately, it needs cheaper energy, competitive industrial inputs, a broader export base, and policies that encourage investment. Textile exports must move towards higher-value products, while IT, agricultural processing, and other tradable sectors need steady support. The real test is to build an economy that can finance more of its own needs.
Published in Dawn, October 18th, 2026
