title: Persistence of force
author: none@none.com (Tariq Parvez)
content:
WHILE the Balochistan insurgency has been simmering for many decades, in recent years, it seems to be spinning out of control.
In July this year, Balochistan became the country’s most violent province, replacing KP for the first time. Some sources say there were 176 terrorist attacks, killing 438 people, including 127 security personnel, the highest ever in a month. This consistent increase in the insurgency’s lethality and spread implies a major mismatch between the threat and the measures taken to counter it.
One major weakness is the imbalance between using armed force to address the challenge and subordinating the political dimension that sustains it. This begs the question: why do we continue to rely totally on the use of force to combat this insurgency, knowing that it has not worked for decades?
    
Historically, COIN (counter-insurgency) strategies have succeeded only when they struck the right balance between armed force and political measures. At best, force can create the right conditions to end an insurgency, but only politics can use that opening to bring about peace through negotiations. In fact, David Galula, in his book Counterinsurgency Warfare: Theory and Practice, argues that a successful COIN strategy is “80 per cent political and 20pc military”. His “First Law of COIN” is that “the support of the population is as necessary for the counterinsurgent as the insurgent”, and that this support can be achieved only through political measures. Similarly, Rupert Smith, in his book The Utility of Force: The Art of War in the Modern World, defines insurgency as “a war amongst people”. He points out the strategic error of using armed force in an insurgency in a way that alienates the local population, reducing the utility of the force used. Thus, local support is crucial to maximising the utility of armed force in dealing with an insurgency and giving the counter-insurgents the upper hand.
Two broad narratives currently shape the Baloch insurgency. The first one, led by Baloch political leaders like Akhtar Mengal and Dr Abdul Malik Baloch (both heads of political parties and former chief ministers of Balochistan), emphasises that the insurgency in Balochistan is predominantly a political problem and requires a political approach for resolution. The second narrative — the military-led state view — which is being implemented in Balochistan is based on the premise that the Baloch insurgency is essentially sponsored by hostile foreign intelligence agencies, and local grievances are of secondary importance. At a workshop on Balochistan at GHQ last year, the military leadership pointed out that foreign-sponsored proxies continually sought to fuel violence and undermine stability in Balochistan. They would be met with a firm response by the military, it was said. This fundamental difference in the threat assessment of the Baloch insurgency between the establishment and the local political leadership leads to divergent responses.
    
The externalisation of the insurgency in Balochistan explains the state’s predominant use of force. Framing the Baloch insurgency as being solely driven by Indian agencies makes it a part of the broader Pakistan-India hostility, and hence defines it as a security threat and not a political challenge. This narrative, naturally, supports a purely coercive response. Interestingly, as a response to the spike in violence in Balochistan in 2026, the state has responded by adding another command to FC Balochistan — with no concomitant political initiatives.
Two broad narratives currently shape the Baloch insurgency.
Indeed, there is much weight in the establishment’s assertion regarding external support to the Baloch insurgents, which is backed by solid evidence, such as the arrest of Indian agent Kulbhushan Jadhav. But to say that the insurgency is totally Indian-supported would be downplaying the significance of the local grievances, which sustain it. This makes our existing COIN strategy in Balochistan lopsided. Two factors strengthen the argument that the insurgency is grounded in local conditions.
One, the triggers of the first four waves of Baloch insurgency were local — in 1948 (annexation of Kalat), 1958 (setting up of One Unit, which erased Balochistan as a political entity, and the arrest of Khan of Kalat), 1962-69 (continued One Unit centralisation, new cantonments in Marri/ Bugti areas and Ayub Khan’s repression), and 1973-77 (dismissal of the NAP government by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto). Second, the current insurgency wave has been going on for more than 20 years now, and to sustain it, a regular stream of local recruits, leadership, and support networks is needed. Such an elaborate network, working clandestinely, carrying out violent acts and hunted by the state, could not sustain itself without strong local support.
That is not to say the state did not try to tap the political dimension. But the endeavour was sporadic, half-hearted, lacked political ownership, and was abandoned too soon. For instance, in 2015, the political and military leadership decided to launch Pur Aman Balochistan — a three-dimensional initiative comprising talks with militants under the leadership of the then chief minister, Dr Malik, some development projects, and an amnesty for certain categories of militants. Dr Malik contacted different leaders, such as Brahmdagh Bugti, and brought back their response. The talks were given up when Dr Malik’s tenure ended the same year. Other parts of this initiative also tapered off because the government showed little interest.
Thus, the persistence of the use of force in Balochistan is primarily due to the framing of this insurgency as a proxy war of hostile countries, and not as an expression of local discontent. This threat assessment does not seem to be working. Carl von Clausewitz in On War states: “The most far-reaching act of judgement that any commander has to make is to establish … the kind of war on which they are embarking.” Because we cannot control it with our current strategy, we must review our assessment of the kind of “war amongst people” we are fighting in Balochistan. Is it an exclusively foreign proxy war or the violent response of radicalised, disgruntled elements of Balochistan, exploited by hostile external elements? Today’s answer will determine whether we can resolve the situation or whether it will become a ‘forever insurgency’.
The writer is a former police officer who was Nacta’s first national coordinator.

topic: Balochistan Insurgency: Causes, Narratives, and Counter-Insurgency Strategies
whyMatters: This article critically analyzes the enduring Balochistan insurgency, highlighting the shortcomings of solely kinetic approaches. Aspirants can use its arguments and references to provide a nuanced perspective on internal security challenges and effective state responses.
summary: The Balochistan insurgency is escalating, indicating a critical mismatch between the threat and current counter-measures, making it the country's most violent province in recent times.
A major weakness in the state's strategy is the imbalance between relying on armed force and subordinating the essential political dimension required to resolve the insurgency.

Two dominant narratives shape the insurgency: one views it as a political problem requiring political solutions (local leadership), while the other frames it primarily as foreign-sponsored, justifying a coercive military response (state/military view).

Despite evidence of external support, local grievances and historical triggers are crucial for the insurgency's persistence and local support networks, making the current state's COIN strategy lopsided.

Successful counter-insurgency (COIN) strategies, as argued by experts like David Galula and Rupert Smith, emphasize that population support, gained through political measures, is paramount, with force creating conditions for political resolution.

David Galula's 'First Law of COIN' states that population support is as necessary for the counterinsurgent as for the insurgent, arguing for '80pc political and 20pc military' strategy.

Historical triggers for earlier Baloch insurgencies included the 1948 annexation of Kalat, 1958 One Unit implementation, 1962-69 centralisation policies, and the 1973-77 dismissal of the NAP government.

title: Terror & governance
author: none@none.com (Dr Raashid Wali Janjua)
content:
EFFECTIVE governance is the best antidote to terrorism. The state’s counterterrorism response has to showcase its best governance practices, including kinetic and non-kinetic means. Terrorism is like a disease that proliferates when it gets a propitious environment. Public frustrations, lack of livelihood, lax policing, and an administrative vacuum serve as the perfect palette for the spread of terrorism.
The merged districts of KP have been affected by a prolonged wave of terrorism, because of which the full range of development and economic initiatives could not be delivered. These areas, wracked by terrorism since the early 2000s, have seen instability due to cross-border movement during the Taliban resistance era of 2003-2021, and an influx of terrorists after 2021.
The hurried US withdrawal left Afghanistan in the hands of a Taliban regime with a mediaeval outlook on statecraft as well as interstate relations. Terrorist entities like the TTP that were pushed out from the merged districts through a series of military operations culminating in Operation Zarb-i-Azb, staged a comeback in 2021 after the US departure. Contrary to Pakistan’s expectations, the Afghan Taliban regime’s policy towards the TTP was driven through a mix of considerations, which included ideological kinship, ethnic affinity, internal power struggles, and an instrument to exert leverage on its neighbour.
The TTP had internalised a belief which treated the US withdrawal as a great victory for the Afghan Taliban that needed to be replicated in Pakistan. They, therefore, got emboldened and refused to abjure violence. Despite an attempt by the government of Pakistan to co-opt them in the national mainstream, the TTP demanded the reversal of Fata’s merger and a governance structure alien to Pakistan’s Constitution. Misplaced rapprochement with the TTP led to a new wave of terrorism in KP’s merged districts that gradually spread to the settled areas. Terrorist attacks in KP shot up thereafter.
Extraordinary times call for extraordinary steps.
LEAs in KP required full government support for acting against the TTP terrorists who had started operating from secure sanctuaries in Afghanistan as well as selected spaces within Pakistan’s merged districts. Single-minded focus was required for kinetic CT operations which, however, was missing in a provincial government consumed by agitational politics. Community mobilisation by public representatives was also stymied due to the confrontational stance of the provincial government against the centre.
Several measures to improve the development and governance aspects in the merged districts were needed, which were not accorded desired priority. These measures included capacity building of the police, establishment of the judicial infrastructure, strengthening the CTD apparatus, and the economic integration of merged districts into the rest of Pakistan. The National Action Plan was also not fully implemented. 
The nexus between crime and terrorism remained unchecked. No effort was made to connect the masses in the merged districts with the state through alternative livelihood opportunities after a crackdown on smuggling and the closure of border trade. According to research statistics of an Islamabad-based think tank, 72 per cent of the terrorists killed in CT operations were below 30 years, while 65pc of them were illiterate or primary qualified, and 66pc jobless.
In the absence of much-needed synergy between the provincial government and the LEAs, CT efforts remained fragmented and desultory, giving space to terrorists to peddle their na-rrative. A prov­i­n­­­cial governme­­nt whose energ-
ies were consu­med by rhetoric, political wrangling, and agitational marches, could not keep its eye on the ball to fight the difficult battle against terrorism. Without single-minded focus, clarity of objectives and sincerity of purpose, the hydra-headed monster of terrorism cannot be slayed.
The Irish example is relevant to KP’s war on terrorism. In Ireland, the conviction rate of terrorists was abysmally low while their mystique was alluring for a population sympathetic to the heroic status of the Irish Republican Army cadres. The British government introduced a package of reforms by building police capacity and picking the best officer, given the title of ‘chief constable’, as a lead terrorism responder, keeping the army in reserve. The judiciary was strengthened through Diplock courts, where the identity of the judges was concealed for their protection. These reforms broke the back of terrorism and the IRA opted for the Good Friday Agreement.
Extraordinary times call for extraordinary steps. If a government does not wish to confront the clear and present danger to the life and property of its people, then it should make way for a dispensation capable of undertaking the difficult task abdicated by it. 
The writer has a PhD degree from Nust.

title: GenZ for mangroves
author: none@none.com (Bina Shah)
content:
MY expository writing class consists of students who will choose one of four interdisciplinary majors: social development studies, politics, philosophy and economics, Asian and Middle Eastern studies, and environmental science. Gen Z has grown up in the shadow of the Covid pandemic; my students are now studying the nightmare of climate change and the ill effects it will have on Pakistan.
Recently, they read a report by Waqas Ali Ranjha in this paper on how mangrove cutting for land reclamation in the Korangi creek is putting the environment in danger. The students were horrified to hear how land grabbers have built an illegal dyke in the Korangi Mangrove Forest, next to the Korangi Biodiversity Park that opened just last year. This dyke blocks water from reaching the mangroves, which will die and be cut down by encroachers. The Sindh Forestry Department confirmed this illegal activity, but the matter is sub judice, and the police will not act.
Mayor Murtaza Wahab had asked the public for feedback about the Biodiversity Park, so I tasked my students with composing ‘letters to the editor’ — a classic exercise for university students to “compliment, critique, inform, or communicate information” on a topic they’re passionate about.
We keep telling these students that they are responsible for finding the solutions to our manmade problems. They know the importance of the mangroves to Karachi’s coastline, protecting it from floods, storms, and rising sea levels. They fear for the destruction of the mangrove’s unique ecosystem, with its birds, animals, and plants that represent the many miracles of the natural world. Alisha Shah writes, “What bothers me is how calculated the whole thing is ... at this rate we’re going to lose a piece of Karachi that we can’t really get back.” Enara Muluk adds, “We already have very little greenery left in Karachi, so we should at least try to protect the mangroves that are still there.”
Students are concerned about the loss of forest cover.
These students note contradictions in the legal process that benefit criminals and miscreants while harming our natural resources. For example, Ayesha Baig asks smartly, “How come the [sub judice order] only applied to the Sindh Forest Department when it came to the removal of the bunds and not to those who are making those bunds?” She urges the public to act, citing previous activist movements like India’s 1970s Chipko Movement where women villagers hugged trees to stop deforestation; and the Sundarbans Protection Struggles, where activists recommend a combination of local knowledge and smart governance to protect an endangered mangrove forest in Bengal.
Some of my students are concerned not just about the environmental impacts of losing the Korangi mangroves, but the livelihoods of fishermen and the resulting economic loss. “Mangroves serve as indispensable ‘nurseries’ for more than 75 per cent of Pakistan’s commercially viable fish, shrimp, and crab species,” writes Faiz Ahmed. “Karachi’s fishing exports are estimated to have a market value around $500 million; a substantial loss in the wildlife population is reflected in these companies’ bottom lines. And the consumers ... have to pay with their wallet as … the price of that once affordable prawn biryani more closely resembles that of a lobster thermidor.”
Destroying the mangroves will have adverse effects on Karachi in other ways, too. Mangroves entrap carbon dioxide, especially relevant in Korangi where factories pollute the air. “If we destroy mangrove ecosystems,” writes Hasnat Alam, “the stored greenhouse gases will be released back into the air. This also weakens Karachi’s ability to [withstand] pollution and to cool the city from heat islands, and it makes urban life less pleasant overall.”
But what should be done about this particular disaster unfolding in slow motion before us? The students want the illegal bund to be removed immediately, despite the sub judice order. Muhammed Ayaz says, “Legal disputes should be resolved through proper judicial procedures, but they should not become an excuse for irreversible environmental damage.” Shah Sarbaz Ali Rehmat writes that the authorities must “disclose the Environmental Impact Assessment for this activity, and designate Korangi Creek as a protected zone”. Meanwhile, Fatima Rubi advises the use of satellite technology and community-based monitoring to look for changes in the mangrove cover.
I can’t think of anyone who would disagree with Syed Riaz Hussein’s call to action: “Stop the cutting, stop the landfilling, and let the water flow back to the mangroves so they can survive and natural life can be sustained.” Hopefully, the mayor, the Sindh Forestry Department, and the police can be convinced to act fast before the damage is done. After all, as Muhammed Ayaz writes, prevention is preferable to restoration.
The writer teaches Expository Writing at AKUFAS.
Published in Dawn, October 16th, 2026

title: Hunger in Pakistan
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S position as the country most affected by hunger in South Asia is not surprising. An economy battered by weather-related disasters, persistent food inflation, weak growth, terrorism, poverty, and joblessness cannot ensure that its people eat enough and well. The findings of the 2026 Global Hunger Index reveal the inadequacy of our economic, agricultural and social policies. Food insecurity is not simply a problem of inadequate agricultural production, but also of access and affordability. The availability of food in the market matters little to families whose incomes cannot keep pace with the prices. Weak farm productivity, inadequate water management, poor storage, post-harvest losses, and flawed market arrangements have long undermined the food system. High input costs, disrupted livelihoods, and falling purchasing power have made nutritious food difficult for poorer households to afford.
Climate change compounds these pressures. Repeated floods destroy crops, livestock, homes, and rural livelihoods. Droughts, erratic rainfall, and rising temperatures threaten harvests. Farmers face risks alongside costly agricultural inputs and uncertain returns. The resulting losses push up food prices, reduce rural incomes, and increase dependence on relief. Policies that fail to encourage investment in modern farming, improve yields or protect farmers’ incentives leave production vulnerable. The human cost is particularly severe for children. The GHI notes that undernourishment has worsened since 2018, and child wasting has moved towards the high threshold. Persistent malnutrition damages physical growth, cognitive development, and future earning capacity. Hunger, therefore, perpetuates poverty and poor productivity across generations. The government must move beyond temporary subsidies. Social protection must reach households that cannot afford basic nutrition, particularly during disasters and price shocks. Besides productive agriculture, climate-resilient infrastructure, better water management, reduced food wastage, and stronger rural employment, lasting progress demands sustained investment in maternal and child nutrition, clean water and primary healthcare.

title: The real reset
author: none@none.com (Tariq Khosa)
content:
IN times like this, we need people who tell hard truths while insisting that the present state of our politics is not permanent. On the one hand, White House aide Stephen Miller says that “we live in a world that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power”, and on the other, philosopher Hannah Arendt says that “out of the barrel of a gun grows the most effective command, resulting in the most instant and perfect obedience. What never can grow out of it is power”. In her 1970 book On Violence, Arendt stresses that violence is not a form of power but its opposite. According to her, power is collective, consensual and relational. By contrast, violence is instrumental and coercive; its strength evaporates the moment the threat is evaded or withdrawn. “Violence can always destroy power,” she concludes.
Pakistan’s present rulers seem to follow Thucydides’ thought: “The strong do what they can, and the weak suffer what they must.” Against this backdrop, they want to reset the collapsed system of governance, according to the minister in charge of internal security and cricket affairs that show clear signs of deterioration. Instead of taking responsibility, he has blamed others for the system’s rot. During his tenure, the security situation in Balochistan and KP has deteriorated significantly. Moreover, widespread violence was witnessed in AJK before the recent polls there.
The first move to reset the system was to promulgate governor’s rule and proclaim an indefinite emergency in a province where an opposition political party with strong public support had been in power since early 2024. The reasons given are couched in a security narrative. The KP government had failed to control the tide of terrorism since it was at the helm of affairs during the last two to three years. The TTP had unleashed terror in the province, especially in five key border districts on the Afghan border.
Many tribal jirgas and multiparty forums held by the provincial legislature opposed the military operations and the use of drone technology that resulted in civilian casualties and population displacement. The protest march led by the chief minister was a political move to persuade the ruling elite to adhere to the Islamabad High Court and Supreme Court decisions to allow access to the incarcerated founder of their party. The SC had directed the prisoner to be treated in a private hospital, in the presence of his physicians and family members. Those court orders were flouted. A simple, humane gesture of following the court’s directions would have defused the political tension between the ruling elite and the opposition parties. Two mainstream parties have lost out the most in the KP fiasco: the PML-N and PPP.
The security situation in Balochistan is far more daunting. Why is there no governor’s rule or emergency there?
The security situation in Balochistan is far more daunting. There, the state faces an armed insurgency in Baloch-dominated areas. The number of terrorist incidents over the last two years is higher than in KP, and the level of violence against the state agencies, including the police, civil armed forces, and the military, is far more serious than anywhere else. Why is there no governor’s rule or emergency there? The answer is simple: the governing administration there is aligned with the establishment. A security strategy based on force has alienated the Baloch youth from the state. Even the Pakhtun areas close to the Afghan and KP borders are reeling under the onslaught of terrorist organisations that are exploiting internal fissures in the two provinces.
Here, we must ask a basic question: what kind of governance structure should dominate Pakistan? Should it be the constitutional order envisioned by the country’s founders, where every citizen is equal under the law, due process is respected, and all institutions act within their legal bounds? Or should Pakistan remain an eternal security state, where justice, lawmaking, foreign policy, the economy, and internal affairs are militarised? A state can justify its power in three ways: by promoting shared values rather than imposing a narrative; by ensuring the sanctity of the electoral process and the rule of law; and by establishing performance legitimacy. The present ruling elite struggles to pass this test. The current governance model needs a reset. Here is how to do it.
First, true representation can emerge only through fair and free elections. A state machinery that cannot hold free elections loses credibility and citizens’ trust. Parliament must represent the people’s will. We need a new and independent election commission. Internal stability and cohesion will remain elusive if questions about the legitimacy of the ruling set-up persist. Only a renewed and fair public mandate at this stage can settle these questions.
Second, centralised control must be replaced with genuine provincial autonomy and strong local self-government. We must adhere to the letter and spirit of the original 1973 Constitution, as the promise of provincial autonomy was the cornerstone of the near-consensus social contract between the state and society.
Third, the independence of the judiciary must be restored by genuine representatives in the new parliament elected through fair mid-term polls. The judiciary’s role in upholding the rule of law and fair administration of justice is crucial to a democratic state.
Fourth, our premier federal intelligence agencies appear to be operating outside the legal fra­m­ework. This lack of accountability must be ad­­d­ressed through parliamentary oversight and laws that clearly define the role of the agencies in both the internal and external security dimensions.
Fifth, terrorism and violent extremism should be addressed by faithfully adhering to the updated CT NAP in 2021 through a long-term, sustainable strategy that invests in non-kinetic measures to address these challenges. Short-term kinetic military operations must be followed by multi-stakeholder, whole-of-society engagement strategies and action plans.
Finally, a meaningful reset can happen only if the security state does not involve itself in political matters. 
The writer is a former police officer.
Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

title: Imaginary justice
author: none@none.com (Rafia Zakaria)
content:
ON any given day, newspaper headlines across Pakistan are littered with updates on court cases. These usually fall into two categories. The first are updates on cases involving political leaders in prison: so and so is brought out for a hearing, so and so has a case stayed. The second category comprises criminal cases that have, largely owing to social media, attracted some attention. Many involve female victims who were killed or raped, sometimes both. Dead women are a topic of interest in Pakistan — much more so than living women. 
There is, however, a third category of cases. These belong to ordinary people — everyday folk who, often erroneously, imagine that Pakistan’s court system can actually deliver justice. The statistics are alarming. According to the Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan, more than 2.2 million cases were pending in Pakistani courts at the end of December 2025. Most of these are civil cases, and if you are unlucky enough to have to file one, you may wait years, sometimes decades, for a final resolution. An entire generation can be conceived, born and raised before your inheritance dispute with your siblings is resolved. 
According to one research paper that analysed the backlog, reasons for delays include frequent adjournments, shortages of judicial officers, inadequate process serving, improper working environments, poor record-keeping facilities, and few resources to run the courts.
Justice, obviously, is not a priority for Pakistan’s rulers. It is not surprising then that the World Justice Project, which issues an annual report on the rule of law in various countries, ranked Pakistan 130th out of 143 countries in 2025. Pakistan was thus among the 14 lowest-ranked countries for adherence to the rule of law. 
Accountability, quite obviously, is a fantasy.
The situation, and the mental picture of thousands and thousands of files piled high with millions of people awaiting justice, is reminiscent of Charles Dickens’ Bleak House, which tells the story of a case that went on for decades. Portions of the opening paragraph read: “Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.”
Fog in Dickens’ narrative stands not simply for the weather phenomenon but also for the murky opacities of a convoluted justice system. More appropriately, a parallel could be drawn with the smog that often settles over Pakistani cities. Smog — a consequence of environmental impurities and societal apathy — has nowhere to go so it suspends itself over human life and can be enumerated in the millions of untended files pushed from hearing to hearing. Sometimes a judge is unavailable, sometimes the lawyers are absent. The emphasis is on everyone except the poor, hapless souls who imagined that justice was a possibility.
The smog, of course, is a metaphor, but it points to lived truths about life in Pakistan. If you are an ordinary person, you live a life on the defensive. When you leave your house, you carry only hope and a prayer. If something goes wrong — your parked car gets hit by a passing truck, your phone is stolen, someone attacks you — you realise just how vulnerable you are. No one will replace your car or your phone, and if your attacker can bribe law enforcers with a bigger pile of cash than you can offer to have them file an FIR, then no one will care about that either. Accountability, quite obviously, is a fantasy. 
All this illustrates how the inability to count on a fu­­nctioning le­­g­al system creates a con­­tor-
ted society that functions ac­­c­ording to the crudest calculations of po­­w­­er. The inability to obtain justice does not simply impede your ability to recover money owed to you or resolve an inheritance dispute. It also means that in any interaction, calculations are made about who has more power and who has less. If a middle-class person has the misfortune of getting into a dispute with someone very wealthy, it is not law that will determine the outcome; it is power. 
Solutions like model courts and alternative dispute resolution mechanisms have been thrown at the problem. These have not resolved the underlying structural weaknesses. Pakistan’s courts do not fail simply because there is a need for more courts or another mechanism for resolving disputes. 
They fail, the argument goes, because powerful Pakistanis — those who draw their power from wealth or brute force — do not believe in the rule of law. 
The consequence is a legal system that serves as a gloss to disguise the crimes of the powerful while the weak remain cowed and tortured by the failures of a sham system. 
The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.

Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

title: After the emergency
author: none@none.com (Ahmed Bilal Mehboob)
content:
THE much-anticipated, and somewhat dreaded, emergency in KP was finally proclaimed by the president on Oct 11. The federal cabinet’s recommendation, the summary of the prime minister’s advice to the president, and the proclamation — all three momentous developments — occurred on the same day. The subsequent actions like taking the chief minister — non-functional but still the elected chief minister of the province — into preventive custody by his subordinate police from within the chief minister’s official residence along with many other senior elected officials; transfer and posting of senior and mid-level Civil Service officials; formation of an advisory council to help the governor in his newly acquired functions; the advisory council’s first meeting and the convening of the meeting of the long-neglected provincial apex committee took place within 48 hours of the proclamation, indicating that the federal government had done its homework in anticipation of the proclamation.
Besides debating whether the emergency would be imposed or not, the media had also been speculating about the specific article in Part X ‘Emergency Provisions’ of the Constitution that would be finally invoked. Articles 232 and 234 were the ‘favourites’ on TV talk shows and, in the end, the federal government did not disappoint either group betting on the choice of articles, as the proclamation invoked both Article 232 and 234. It seems that the government was not taking any chances. While Article 232 was apparently favoured because it does not set a limit on the period of emergency, it contains a ‘flaw’ in the federal government’s view, as it does not bar the provincial assembly from functioning during the period of emergency under Article 232. The federal government simultaneously invoked Article 234 apparently to render the provincial assembly non-functional during the emergency and to vest all legislative powers in parliament. Invoking both articles simultaneously appears to be unprecedented, although an emergency has been proclaimed about seven times in Pakistan since the adoption of the 1973 Constitution. This manifests the hard line with which the federal government wants to implement the proclamation of emergency.
In most media reports, Article 232 has been frequently referred to as the instrument to proclaim emergency, in contrast to Article 234 that, according to these reports, has been used to proclaim governor’s rule. A plain reading of the Constitution, however, does not bear out this distinction. Both articles concern the proclamation of an emergency, and both give the federal government the option to either exercise executive powers directly in the province or designate the provincial governor to do so on its behalf. Article 234 is invoked either on a report from the provincial governor to the president, or after the two Houses of parliament separately pass a resolution asking the president to proclaim an emergency under Article 234. The president may or may not act based on the governor’s report. Still, if the two Houses pass a resolution to this effect, the president must invoke Article 234.
Both articles lay down different requirements for parliamentary approval of the proclamation. Article 232 requires that the proclamation be laid before the two Houses for approval by each within 10 days of the proclamation if the latter has been made by the president on his own (which is the case for the emergency proclaimed on Oct 11), and not based on a resolution passed by the provincial assembly. The federal government easily fulfilled this requirement on Oct 14, despite the fiery speeches and the opposition’s subsequent boycott of the proceedings. Article 232 also provides that the proclamation issued under the article be laid before a joint sitting of the two Houses within 30 days. This formality was also fulfilled.
The government might survive constitutional challenges, but can face political risks.
Article 234 simply requires that the proclamation issued under the article be laid before a joint sitting of parliament. The proclamation will cease to be valid at the end of two months unless the joint sitting extends the validity by another two months. The joint sitting is authorised to grant up to two extensions of two months each, meaning the proclamation of emergency under this article can continue for a maximum of six months. Given the clear majority of the ruling coalition and the PPP, continuing the proclamation of emergency under this article for six months doesn’t seem to pose a challenge for the federal government. The provincial assembly will become functional after six months, but, as seen in the past, federal governments manage to engineer such a change within the assembly during this period that it doesn’t pose a major challenge to the centre. This is more likely because the provincial government will remain non-functional indefinitely under Article 232.
While the federal government may be able to surmount constitutional challenges, it might still face serious political difficulties. Although contrary to the warnings of the non-functional chief minister of KP and other PTI leaders, no serious agitation has been witnessed in the country or even in KP so far, it should cause some discomfort to the federal government that none of the political parties other than those in the ruling coalition has supported the proclamation.
Articles 232 and 234 do not restrain the high court’s powers, but a serious judicial challenge appears unlikely. However, the majority of proclamations of emergency challenged in the courts previously could not be sustained.
Last but probably not least, the federal government and the security establishment have put their prestige at stake by taking on total responsibility to combat and defeat terrorism in the province. After the proclamation of emergency, there is no longer a provincial government to blame for the rising arc of terrorism. 
The writer is the president of Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.

title: Diplomatic options
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
AS Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi movement continue to trade fire, and the US-Iran war is locked in a stalemate, regional states continue to stress the need for a diplomatic solution to the conflicts in both theatres. Numerous attempts have been made in the past to find a negotiated off-ramp in both conflicts, but they have met with little success.
Regional states know that the alternative to talks — a fully fledged war on both fronts — will bring immeasurable destruction to the Gulf, the Red Sea and the surrounding areas. The need for diplomacy was stressed during Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi’s visit to Pakistan on Wednesday. Though the visit was of a bilateral nature, the regional situation was high on the agenda, with Oman’s top diplomat reiterating that “diplomacy is the only way forward”.
Both Pakistan and Oman have played integral roles in trying to find a negotiated settlement to the US-Iran dispute, while the sultanate is also a key link between the Saudis and the Houthis. Both Pakistan and Oman know that any further escalation either in the Gulf or in Yemen will destabilise the whole region.
    
With regard to the Yemeni conflict, while Pakistan has pledged to stand “shoulder to shoulder” with Saudi Arabia, the prospect of a long war of attrition involving the kingdom and its allies, and the pro-Iran Houthis, is in no one’s interest. The goal, therefore, should be a renewed ceasefire, which promises Saudi security and an end to the Yemeni civil war. Pakistan, Oman and other regional states should concentrate on achieving this goal.
Where Iran is concerned, it is likely that the US will make its next move after the midterm elections in early November. However, media reports that America plans on dropping the ‘mother of all bombs’ on Iranian energy and nuclear sites should be a matter of concern for all. America’s aggression has failed to make Iran capitulate, and it is hard to see what more violence will achieve, other than perpetuating chaos in the region.
What is needed is a holistic ceasefire that addresses all fronts — Iran, Yemen, Lebanon — along with a long-term peace between the US and Iran. The US must also refrain from initiating more wars in the Middle East, along with reining in its bloodthirsty ally Israel.

title: Strengthening LGs
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE ECP has done well to refuse to allow the Punjab administration to push the local government elections to April. It should now hold its ground. Four years after the last elected councils left office, the province is still looking for reasons not to hold the polls. The reasons, though, keep changing. In August, the provincial authorities agreed to a window between Dec 15 and Jan 15. Two months later, they discovered that the months of December and January are foggy and cold, and that Ramazan would begin in February. None of this is news. Winter arrives every year, and the Ramazan calendar was not a surprise to anyone who signed off on the August consultations. LGs are the tier of the state closest to the people. They handle sanitation, water supply, street lighting, primary health and schooling, and local roads, and generally keep the town running. In functioning democracies, this is where citizens learn to hold someone accountable, and where future political leaders learn to govern. Provincial and federal parties know this, and many are uncomfortable with the fact. An elected mayor with a budget and a mandate is a rival centre of power. A commissioner or deputy commissioner who answers to the chief minister is not. So elections are delayed, laws rewritten whenever the government changes, and administrators fill the space that elected representatives should occupy.
The Constitution requires each province to set up an LG system and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility, and authority to its elected representatives. Holding elections is only the first step. Every provincial government, especially Punjab, has treated even that step as optional, and the ones that have held elections have often hollowed out the institutions afterwards. Councils without control over their own funds, staff or functions are decorative. This matters more now than it did before. The debate on improving governance by creating new provinces has gathered pace, and it rests on a sound observation. Provinces are too centralised to serve their citizens from afar. A new provincial map, however, will not help. The new provinces will continue to behave like the old ones, hoarding power and funds at the top. If the aim is better governance, the more direct route is to strengthen the tier that already exists in the Constitution but has never been allowed to work.
Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

title: Don’t derail the transition
author: none@none.com (Ishrat Husain)
content:
PAKISTAN has reached a staff-level agreement with the IMF after completing the fourth review under its programme. Implementation of the Extended Fund Facility is on track, with progress on macroeconomic stability. The challenge is to translate the gains into sustained growth.
Political and administrative disruptions that can derail this difficult transition must be avoided. The fiscal deficit has been contained at 2.6 per cent of GDP. The primary surplus has strengthened, supported by provincial cash surpluses and exceptional grants to the federal budget. Revenue targets have been met, though raising petroleum levies amid rising global prices adds to inflationary pressure. The external current account has been broadly balanced, largely because of stronger-than-expected workers’ remittances, despite declining merchandise exports.
Sovereign credit ratings have improved, though remaining below 2006-07 levels. Access to global capital markets for long-term financing stands restored, and diversification into instruments like Panda bonds has begun. Foreign portfolio inflows have recovered, but FDI remains disappointing. Talks with the US Treasury on a proposed 10-year Exchange Stabilisation Facility continue, while tariff reduction discussions with the US Trade Representative remain inconclusive.
Foreign exchange reserves accumulated by purchasing dollars from the intermarket rather than borrowing now cover three months of imports, up from a trough of $4.3 billion in FY2023, helping stabilise the exchange rate and strengthen the balance of payments.
External public debt has declined to 25pc of GDP; the share of short-term debt has fallen from 24 to 16pc, partly after a Saudi deposit was converted into a three-year facility.
Yet ordinary citizens see little improvement. Poverty, joblessness, poor public services, unfair taxation, intrusive regulation, and high energy prices constrain households and businesses. Savings and investment are weak, and exports lack the dynamism to sustain growth. We must expand productive capacity, employment, and exports without reigniting inflation or destabilising the external account. This requires completing the structural reform agenda. Federal and provincial governments must be right-sized, civil services professionalised through specialist recruitment and better incentives, and public administration digitised. The FBR must broaden the tax base instead of burdening compliant taxpayers; provinces must effectively implement agriculture income and property taxes. Energy and wheat markets must be made more competitive, with BISP protection for poor households.
Restructuring and privatising SOEs, reforming the Export Facilitation Scheme, implementing the National Tariff Policy, and expanding financial access for small businesses, farmers, women entrepreneurs, and housing are equally important. Export financing and insurance must reach new exporters. Delays or reversals will weaken investment, employment, and competitiveness, undermining the stability painstakingly achieved. Long-delayed infrastructure projects must advance — the Karachi-Peshawar ML-1 railway, the Sukkur-Hyderabad motorway, oil pipeline extensions, oil refinery upgrades, the Quetta-Zhob highway, five special industrial zones, and revamping the Karachi Circular Railway. Skills upgrading must complement these investments.
Pakistan is midway from crisis management to sustainable growth.
Industrial, automobile, and strategic trade policies must be harmonised in consultation with the private sector and announced without delay. A credible implementation framework with clear milestones, assigned duties, and firm timelines is needed. Regular monitoring, inter-agency coordination, and timely bottleneck removal must rep­lace announcements without execution. External risks make the transition more urgent.
The US-Iran war, disruptions to energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, and instability in Bab el-Mandeb can sharply raise import costs, intensifying uncertainty over inflation, the current account and exchange rate. Suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty compounds water insecurity. Meanwhile, AI is transforming labour markets, creating uncertainty about job opportunities.
Against this backdrop, three domestic sources of disruption demand particular attention. First, security in KP and Balochistan must be restored through dialogue and an effective counterterrorism strategy. Poverty and conflict reinforce each other. Reversals in poverty reduction are linked to conflict-affected districts, where social indicators are among the weakest nationally. The NFC framework should give greater weight to disadvantaged districts, alongside empowered local governments (LGs). Federal and provincial governments must jointly own a practical CT plan. The apex committees set up after 2014 showed the value of coordinated action in restoring peace. Imposing emergency and governor’s rule in KP could, instead, intensify political tensions and worsen law and order amid terrorist attacks. Economic relief, jobs, and better public services must complement security operations.
Second, the movement of goods and services ac­ross the country must be uninterrupted. LEAs re­­quisitioning containers, trucks, and oil tankers disrupt trade. Imports must reach factories on sc­h­­­­­­edule, exporters must honour delivery comm­it­m­­ents, and farmers must transport perishable pro­­duce to urban markets without delay. Supply disruptions raise prices and create household shortages.
Internet shutdowns are equally damaging, disrupting payments, business transactions, logist­ics, information flows, and the work of freelancers and firms exporting IT and IT-enabled services. Economic activity requires predictable rules and uninterrupted movement of goods, people, and information. Administrative measures intended to address immediate security concerns must not impose disproportionate costs on the economy.
Third, the debate over new provinces/ administrative units shouldn’t become another source of instability. It’s a contentious proposal; the Sindh Assembly has opposed dividing the province. Administrative reorganisation requires constitutional clarity, fiscal assessment, and political consensus. Failing to do so would divert scarce resources to new bureaucracies, increase administrative expenditure, and weaken provincial cash surpluses transferred to the centre. Fiscal consolidation will then suffer, jeopardising macroeconomic stability. Strengthening LGs and improving service delivery within existing arrangements should take precedence.
Pakistan is midway through a demanding transition from crisis management to sustainable growth. Political leaders hope that the present IMF programme will be the country’s last. Fulfilling that aim needs continuity, discipline, and determined implementation. External shocks can’t be controlled, but their impact can be mitigated through sound policies and domestic consensus. The priority is clear: restore peace through dialogue, keep goods and services moving, complete reforms already initiated, and avoid divisive experiments. Pakistan can’t afford to squander its hard-won stability through preventable disruptions. The transition to growth must be protected, not derailed.
The writer is a former State Bank governor.
Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

title: Lagging behind
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE IMF’s latest World Economic Outlook projects Pakistan’s economy to grow by 3.5pc in the current fiscal year, while average inflation climbs to 9.9pc. The current account is expected to slip into a deficit of 1pc of GDP. This forecast points to an economy that remains vulnerable despite recent gains in macroeconomic stability.
The economy expanded by 3.6pc last year. Further slowdown matters for a country with a rapidly increasing population, entrenched poverty, and high unemployment. Growth at this pace will hardly raise incomes meaningfully or absorb new entrants into the labour market.
Inflation poses another challenge. After easing to 7.1pc last year, it is forecast to rise sharply, leading to fears of further erosion of purchasing power. For families already squeezed by high energy costs, taxes, and essential expenses, renewed price pressures will undermine any benefits from economic stabilisation. The projected current account deficit signals renewed pressure on foreign exchange earnings.
Higher oil prices and shipping disruptions make imports more expensive. Unless exports grow faster and are more diversified, stronger domestic demand could again widen the external gap. The IMF expects unemployment to decline to 6.5pc in FY27 from 6.9pc the previous year. But, in the absence of stronger growth, which can create a sufficient number of jobs, that is hardly of any comfort. It does not establish whether new jobs will be productive, secure or adequately paid. Nor does it show whether employment is expanding fast enough to keep pace with the working-age population.
The South Asia region is forecast to grow by 6.4pc in 2026. Pakistan’s 3.5pc projection places it far below the regional average, highlighting our failure to build a sustained growth engine. The global picture is also distressing. The IMF forecasts global growth of 3.1pc in 2026, rising to 3.4pc in 2027. Investment in AI is supporting activity in some economies. Others face higher energy costs, trade disruptions, and tighter financial conditions. Growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. We must prepare for these pressures rather than assume that stabilisation will deliver prosperity.
The immediate task is to contain inflation and protect vulnerable households without reviving unsustainable subsidies or excessive demand. For that, the government must shift resources towards productive investment, improve the competitiveness of industry, broaden the tax base and expand export capacity. Better education, skills, and employment opportunities are equally important. These changes require consistent policies, not another short-lived cycle of incentives and concessions. The IMF projections expose the cost of postponing structural reform. An economy growing at 3.5pc, with inflation approaching double digits and a weakening external balance, remains vulnerable to the next shock.
Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

title: Provinces under fire
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
THE liquidation of the KP Assembly is an event rooted in economic, more specifically fiscal, constraints. For the time being, it is unlikely that the trajectory will continue to the other provinces, but it is worth keeping an eye on the resource envelope available to the state as the primary fount of this event.
Here is how it works. Every time the state is faced with a major demand for resources, usually for security-related matters, financial managers point to the NFC Award as the reason why that demand cannot be met. In the middle of the 2010s, for example, the then PML-N government faced a major demand for resources to pay for the military operations underway in the wake of the Army Public School massacre by the TTP. The then finance minister Ishaq Dar had said, in December 2016 for instance, that the government had to spend over Rs300 billion on the security operations since they began. He proposed a cut of seven per cent from the Federal Divisible Pool before provincial shares were calculated, in order to meet the expenses going forward.
The next year, Miftah Ismail, the then special assistant to the prime minister on finance, again pointed to the NFC Award and provincial expenditures as the reason why the federal government had to run such a large budget deficit and why demands for releases from the development budget might have to wait.
That was in October 2017, when Dar was no longer finance minister. In 2019, prime minister Imran Khan told a rally in Ghotki that the 18th Amendment had bankrupted Pakistan, and his government had no resources left to pay for development or relief after paying for debt servicing, defence and transfers to the provinces under the NFC Award.
In 2020, his own information minister was telling TV channels that his government might have to “change the law” on the NFC Awards because its allocations had become unsustainable. In 2024, Miftah Ismail was quoted in Dawn as saying that “the federal government is teetering on the brink of bankruptcy while the provinces are flush with cash”. Shortly afterwards, the current Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb was quoted in Washington, where he had gone for the annual IMF and World Bank meetings, as saying that Islamabad would revisit the NFC Award, if the IMF loan was approved, through either expenditure-sharing or incentives for provinces to widen the tax base.
Many of these people subsequently took their statements back, or at least added caveats that their government had no intention to “roll back” the NFC. The main reason for the backtracking is that every major political party in the country — the PPP, PML-N and PTI — controlled a province, and none wanted to become a party to any attempt to roll back provincial rights.
What began as a search for resources turned into a search for a new political arrangement.
But the litany of complaints about the enhanced provincial shares under the last NFC continued. Ahsan Iqbal repeated them last year in Karachi, and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif publicly floated the idea of changing the composition of the divisible pool, perhaps by removing customs duties from it. This remark triggered a little conversation of its own, with some delving into how and why these duties were part of the divisible pool in the first place. All along, almost from the very first year when the empowered provincial government’s scheme went into effect from 2009, blaming them has become the favourite excuse for failure in Islamabad. But the scheme itself, which consists of the 18th Amendment and the NFC Award, endured because of the power of consensus behind it.
In recent years, though, with the arrival of the ‘hybrid-plus’ government, the conversation around the federative scheme of empowered provinces has turned more menacing. An attempt was made by the federal authorities, for example, to usurp Sindh’s share of water resources, and a demand for some amount of reverse-flow from the provinces to the centre found concrete form in an MoU signed in the NFC meetings as part of the budget for FY27. An amount of Rs1.04 trillion is supposed to be transferred back to the federal government by three provinces — Punjab, Sindh, and KP — this fiscal year.
What began as an economic conversation acquired political and security substance as it rolled through the system. As part of the complaints, questions were raised about what the provinces were doing with the incremental resources flowing their way since 2009. Some demanded to know where we should look for the results. A World Bank report landed in the middle of all this, showing that the bulk of incremental resources was consumed in salaries and other current expenditures, while social indicators showed little to no improvement since the scheme of enhanced provincial powers went into effect. That added fuel to the fire.
What began as a search for resources turned into a search for a new political arrangement, with some in government publicly saying a “reset” was coming. It acquired a security dimension as the PTI government was called upon to play its part in the counterterrorism operations in KP. And it fed an opportunistic suggestion for wrapping up the whole system and bringing in “administrative units” to replace provincial governments altogether.
Somewhere in all this a perception seems to have taken root that the state’s federative structure is too expensive for a resource-starved country like Pakistan. If the provinces have nothing to show for all the funds they have consumed since their powers and resource commitments were enhanced, why keep them longer, ask the proponents of this thinking. They don’t yet have an alternative structure to propose. But in the months to come, it is likely that the governments of Sindh and Punjab will be asked to grant more space to the federal government in the control of the resources they command.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

title: Water is a right, not a weapon
author: Syed Mohammad Ali.
content:
In January, United Nations researchers issued a stark warning: the world has moved beyond a water crisis and into a state of "global water bankruptcy". This warning was issued via a new flagship report from the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health, which also pointed out how decades of overuse and environmental degradation have pushed many rivers, aquifers, lakes, wetlands and glaciers into a post-crisis condition from which their historical 'normal' may no longer be recoverable.

Such a warning could hardly be timelier. Water is becoming increasingly entangled with geopolitics and conflict. In the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on critical infrastructure have highlighted the vulnerability of desalination facilities that supply drinking water to millions across the Gulf. When water infrastructure becomes part of a military confrontation, the consequences extend far beyond the battlefield.

But direct military conflict is not the only danger. Even the mismanagement of water can deepen existing political and social tensions. The Nile has become a source of prolonged tension between Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Environmental degradation around Lake Chad has intensified competition over scarce resources between pastoral and agricultural communities, and enabled Boko Haram to exploit weak governance and socioeconomic marginalisation to increase its influence.

The UN has thus aptly emphasised that water can be a driver of conflict, a weapon of conflict or a casualty of conflict. Conversely, however, water sharing can also serve as a basis for cooperation. It is in this latter context that the militarisation of the Indus river system needs to be understood. India's decision in 2025 to place the Indus Waters Treaty in "abeyance" disrupted a framework that survived several wars and decades of political hostility. While this treaty has several flaws which need to be addressed, suspending a treaty which enables institutional cooperation at a time of accelerating climate stress is especially dangerous.

Climate change is transforming the Himalayan rivers, and the Indus basin is already under immense pressure from rising temperatures, changing precipitation patterns and shifts in snow and glacial melt. The Indus is not simply a river divided between two hostile states. It is part of a rapidly changing cryosphere. Understanding these changes requires continuous scientific observation, hydrological data and cooperation across borders. Yet the deterioration of Indo-Pak relations threatens precisely the mechanisms that could make such knowledge possible.

Whatever disagreements India and Pakistan have over dams, allocations or security, they share a basic interest in knowing what is happening to the rivers and aquifers on which hundreds of millions depend. That means restoring regular hydrological data exchange and creating mechanisms for joint or independently verified monitoring of shared natural resources to better contend with climate impacts.

Moreover, for lower riparian countries such as Pakistan, the problem is not simply that there is too little water. Much of the water available is used inefficiently and distributed inequitably, while investment in drinking water, sewerage and sanitation remains far too weak. A country can therefore have a water-security crisis even while enormous volumes of water continue to flow through its rivers and irrigation systems.

Achieving water security cannot mean only building more dams or trying to control rivers. It must also mean using water efficiently, allocating it fairly, protecting aquifers and watersheds and ensuring that ordinary citizens have reliable access to safe water. Pakistan need not wait for India to restore the Indus Waters Treaty before undertaking these domestic measures.

Achieving water security requires not only international cooperation and data exchange on shared resources but also robust domestic measures focusing on efficient use, equitable allocation, and improved infrastructure for all citizens.

title: Multan derailment
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
IN numerous states, including many of Pakistan’s neighbours, rail transport is a safe and affordable mode of travel. But in this country, rail journeys can be perilous, as the derailment of the Peshawar-bound Rehman Baba Express near Multan early on Tuesday shows. In fact, derailments and accidents are far too common on our rail network, because for decades, the railways have remained underfunded. At least five people died in the tragedy, which is being blamed on “mechanical failure”. The worthy railways minister has said an investigation is under way. There is, of course, much to investigate where the overall state of the rail network is concerned. As per figures in the media, at least 35 train accidents were reported in the first six months of the current year, while in 2025, there were 95 incidents.
The railways authorities say they have been making ‘improvements’, such as digitalising stations, and providing Wi-Fi. But where overhaul is concerned, especially upgrading signalling equipment and tracks, much needs to be done. Pakistan has a plan (ML-1) to bring its railways into the 21st century; what is missing is much of the funding — billions of dollars are required — as well as the will on part of the state to forge ahead with the modernisation plan. Perhaps officialdom is slothful because train transport is no longer used by the elite. The prime minister recently said he wants to see progress on ML-1; a launch date of January 2027 has been announced. However, it should be remembered that several launch dates for the megaproject have come and gone. To ensure the safety of passengers, and make critical upgrades to the national rail network, the authorities must set realistic timelines, arrange the funding, and start work without delay. A modern passenger and freight rail network can bring considerable economic advantages, while improving connectivity internally and with neighbouring states.
Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

The ongoing issues are attributed to systemic mechanical failures and a lack of significant upgrades to crucial infrastructure like signalling equipment and tracks.

The ambitious ML-1 modernization plan, intended to bring railways into the 21st century and enhance regional connectivity, is stalled due to a severe lack of funding (billions of dollars) and insufficient political will.

Timely and adequate investment in railway modernization is essential not only for passenger safety and internal economic benefits but also for improving connectivity with neighboring states, which is foundational for regional integration efforts.

title: Pulling the pin
author: none@none.com (F.S. Aijazuddin)
content:
ONE does not need to have Mao Zedong’s eyes to see that “everything under heaven is in utter chaos”. There is no continent in the world (except perhaps his China) where conditions are in the control of its leaders. In France, for example, students in the country’s lycées, or secondary schools, are demonstrating against “long school days, overcrowded classrooms, outdated facilities, and teacher shortages”. The protesters are 15- to 18-year-olds. They are too young to vote. Yet their anger threatens to detract from the presidential election in early 2027, when France decides who is to replace Emmanuel Macron.
In South America, countries with valuable natural resources and precious minerals are bracing themselves for a raid by the US. If oil-rich Venezuela can be decapitated overnight, can Brazil, Chile and Argentina be far behind? In Ukraine, an embattled Volodymyr Zelensky finds he has now two adversaries — a determined Vladimir Putin, and a mercurial Donald Trump, who has suggested that the Ukrainians “get a new leader who can make a deal”. The abandonment of Zelensky came a day after Trump agreed to buy diesel from Putin.
Historians who will chronicle the decline and fall of Trump’s presidency may do worse than rely upon Edward Gibbon’s memorable analysis: “But the decline of Rome was the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness. Prosperity ripened the principle of decay; the cause of the destruction multiplied with the extent of conquest… . … Instead of inquiring why the Roman Empire was destroyed, we should rather be surprised that it has subsisted for so long.”
In and around the Arabian Peninsula, the US-Israel vs Iran conflict has taken a sinister turn. Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan have entered into a defence pact. Saudi petrodollars have linked arms with Türkiye’s armament capacity and Pakistani martial manpower. It is less a tripartite alliance than a pas de trois of death. Few realise that this tripartite pact has inbuilt weaknesses. The three countries are not territorially contiguous.
Historians may do worse than rely upon Gibbon’s analysis.
This new pact purports to imitate the collective defence clause of Article 5 of Nato, which means that should Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, or Türkiye be individually attacked, the other two will have to spring to the victim’s defence.
Türkiye is a card-carrying member of Nato. If it is involved militarily, all other Nato member countries will be bound to ‘defend’ Türkiye, and, therefore, by extension Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. That is the legal theory. Practically, Nato’s selectivity has already been tested during the Ukraine crisis. Even though Nato did not extend the umbrella of membership to Ukraine, it chose to defend Ukraine (a non-Nato country) against Russia. Obviously, Nato members and Trump follow Machiavelli’s precept: “He who has the power is always right.”
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan share some commonalities. Each has a Sunni majority, and all three currently have governments that are intolerant of domestic opposition.
Recep Erdogan’s government in 2025 imprisoned his most popular rival — Istanbul’s mayor Ekrem Imamoglu. In 2017, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman ordered the detention of over-rich princes and government ministers in the five-star Ritz-Carlton Hotel in Riyadh, where many were allegedly tortured. In 2018, Saudi dissident Jamal Khashoggi was strangled and dismembered by a squad of 15 Saudis (allegedly on the orders of their crown prince) in the Saudi consulate in Istanbul.
And here in our country, a leader and his party members — regardless of gender or age — have been sentenced to imprisonment, without the hope of an amnesty.
Our federal government is in opposition with smaller pro­­vinces — it has im­­­p­­osed an emergency and governor’s rule in KP. Azad Kashmir has had governments drawn from two Pa­­kistani mainstream political parties. The continuing friction brings to mind these lines from Kahlil Gibran’s poignant poem Pity the Nation: “Pity the nation divided into fragments/ each fragment deeming itself a nation.”
Not many leaders have the time nor the wit to read Gibbon’s six-volume work on the Roman Empire, or the Meditations bequeathed by the emperor he admired most — Marcus Aurelius. They should. Core lessons derived from Aurelius point to five signs of a weak mind: ‘Surrendering control to external circumstances; complaining and playing the victim; seeking external validation and obsessing over others’ opinions; letting uncontrolled emotions dictate actions; and resisting the present moment and avoiding duty.’
How many leaders — or even us common folk — would survive such a litmus test?
Many regard the chaos prevailing everywhere as deeply ominous in its implications. The pin has been removed from the grenade. It is only a matter of time before a doomsday detonation.
The writer is an author.

title: Will China beat the US in AI?
author: none@none.com (Asad Baig)
content:
IN China, people are being paid to fold clothes, wipe tables, and open microwave doors. Wearing virtual reality headsets and exoskeletons, they repeat the movements hundreds of times so humanoid robots can learn them. Across China, similar centres have people performing other painfully ordinary tasks. The work looks mundane, but it produces precious data.
It may seem like an odd way to begin a story about geopolitics, but like this piece, it offers im­­portant clues about who is better placed to ‘win’ the AI race — China or the US? The winner will have a much larger say in the next world order.
Donald Trump insists America must win the AI race, a contest his administration has likened to the Cold War’s ‘space race’. The analogy is attractive, but Michael Kratsios, Trump’s science advi­ser, later conceded the obvious problem. Unlike the race to the moon, this one has no finish line.
On the conventional scoreboard, the US rem­ains formidable. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index counts 59 notable American models in 2025 against China’s 35. US private AI investment exceeded China’s 23 times over, though this understates Chinese spending through government funds. Yet the report says the model performance gap has “effectively closed”, as of March 2026, the leading US model was ahead by just 2.7 per cent.
Pakistan does not need to win the AI race. It needs to win from AI.
Frontier models are not the only measure of success. China may be building its advantage by pushing AI into the physical economy.
In March, the US China Economic and Security Review Commission ‘warned’ of a reinforcing lo­­­op in China. Cheap, open models spread into fa­­c­­to­r­ies, logistics, and robotics. Their use generates specialised real-world data, which then imp­roves the models. That could create an advantage proprietary American systems may struggle to mat­ch, even if they remain stronger on benchmarks.
Most importantly, China had classified data as a factor of production in 2020. Factories are paid for access to workers wearing cameras and sensors, while others earn money performing household tasks to train robots.
On the flip side, America’s AI boom grew out of an internet economy built on years of accumulated online content and behavioural data, where major platforms are accused of “vast surveillance” by the FTC, with users having little control over their data’s use.
I am not suggesting China has a better privacy regime. It does not. The point is that China is producing, pricing, and feeding data back into industry, building an ecosystem that could give it an immense edge over the US.
And it already has the machinery. China had more than two million industrial robots operating by 2024 and installed 354,000 in 2025 alone. According to the International Federation of Robotics, China accounted for 59pc of new industrial robot installations worldwide in 2025. The real advantage may, therefore, be the ecosystem itself, ie, factories produce robots, robots produce data, data improves AI, and AI improves factories.
Then comes energy, as I argued earlier in these pages. The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects data centre electricity use to nearly double to 950 terawatt-hours by 2030. Whoever can expand reliable, affordable power fastest will have an edge in building the AI ecosystem.
In the US, data centres are expected to account for nearly half of electricity demand growth to the end of the decade, while natural gas supplies more than 40pc of their electricity. Grid delays are pushing developers towards on-site gas generation. But the IEA says ensuring reliable supply requires generating capacity 30pc to 70pc above demand, while turbine shortages may undermine hopes of getting power faster.
To its advantage, China accounts for around 85pc of global solar supply chain production capacity and 80pc of lithium-ion battery capacity. It added nearly 500 gigawatts of renewable capacity in 2025 alone.
The idea isn’t to romanticise the figurative ‘Chinese model’, considering they still use coal to supply nearly 70pc of the electricity used by Chinese data centres. But their advantage is clear. China manufactures much of the machinery needed to generate and store the next unit of electricity.
However, China still faces weaknesses. It depends on foreign technology across parts of the semiconductor chain, while restrictions on advanced memory are raising domestic chip costs. Chinese firms are nevertheless developing alternatives to Nvidia, seeking to make AI deployment more affordable and reduce dependence on American hardware. The US retains substantial advantages in frontier research, Nvidia’s computing ecosystem and capital, but China is building more of the hardware and software needed for its own ecosystem.
The contest is also moving beyond the two countries. America’s AI Action Plan explicitly seeks to export full-stack US technology packages, including hardware, models, software and standards, whereas China is pushing open models and a competing international architecture.
To summarise, if I had to pick a likely winner in the figurative AI race, I would lean towards China. Its advantage may lie in how effectively it turns AI into industrial strength and economic productivity.
But the obvious question remains: Where does that leave Pakistan?
Pakistan should resist that pressure to choose sides and rethink what it means to become a regional AI leader. Competing in frontier chips, foundation models and vast data centres requires an industrial base we lack. Our scarce resources should go where they can make the greatest difference.
As I argued in ‘Pakistan’s AI checklist’, published in this paper in June, we need reliable power, computing capacity, local hosting for sensitive data, skilled people, local datasets, and rules that protect rights. We should use global tools where they help and build our own capacity where dependence leaves us vulnerable. The purpose of this investment must be clear.
I have said this earlier as well. Pakistan does not need to win the AI race. It needs to win from AI. Helping farmers conserve water, teachers identify learning gaps, businesses become more productive, and public departments reduce waste would achieve more than another announcement about becoming an AI hub.
China’s lesson is that technology becomes power when it translates into productivity. Our greatest risk is becoming little more than a market for systems built elsewhere, with too little capacity to shape how they serve us.
The writer is the founder of Media Matters for Democracy.
