title: The lost civilian CT body
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Amir Rana)
content:
THIS is an obituary for the National Counter Terrorism Authority, once conceived as a civilian counterterrorism body that combined policymaking, coordination among law-enforcement agencies, and data collection and processing.
Since its inception in December 2008, and even after gaining legal cover under the Nacta Act, 2013, it has struggled to fully realise its role and mandate, while facing resistance from LEAs reluctant to coordinate with a police-led body.
Appointing a senior military officer as its national coordinator was not the first deviation from the Nacta Act. A bigger departure from the statute had come in 2025 with the establishment of the National Intelligence Fusion and Threat Assessment Centre. Niftac was created as a parallel body, apparently under Nacta but in effect superior to it, even though Nacta is the statutory body. This gave a superior security institution the leading role.
Nacta’s new form seems to have little to do with developing a counterterrorism strategy, building a coordination mechanism, or taking on a CT-related operational role. Its real purpose is to synchronise all civilian-led LEAs with the superior security institution, and, at the very least, to bring them under one roof. This synchronisation of internal security policy with the security doctrine conceived by the establishment’s top brass has been underway for a long time, taking various forms. Bureaucrats see it in the National Security and War Course (NSWC) at the National Defence University (NDU), which is now equivalent to the National Management Course, a mandatory course for promotion from Grade 20 to 21.
The NSWC gives senior bureaucrats more opportunities to align with evolving thinking at the top levels of the security institutions. At the narrative level, NDU and many other military-led institutions run short courses for opinion-makers, politicians, and business and community leaders to align them with the new thought process. Interestingly, all these courses and discourses happen at the expense of civilian governments, whether provincial or federal.
Nacta, the only civilian-led CT body, struggled to find its role and eventually lost.
One may argue that synchronisation within the internal security structure will improve coordination, the very dream for which Nacta was conceived. However, the new changes appear to be aimed at control, and the CT body is being used as an instrument of that. The structures of other LEAs, such as the police and FIA, leave little room for intervention by other institutions — unlike Nacta.
Admittedly, Nacta had a few good leaders who clearly understood the terrorism challenge facing the country and how to respond. But it is safe to say that most of its heads, and even others who served in the authority, had little idea of the CT body’s objectives. Many came on deputation, or to rest before landing a field posting.
    
As mentioned earlier, Nacta faced pressure and challenges from superior security institutions, which were reluctant to work under or with a civilian-led body. Still, the police cadre is undoubtedly responsible for destroying the institution and providing an excuse for its takeover. This did not happen overnight. The process began much earlier. When former prime minister Imran Khan chaired the Nacta board of governors meeting in September 2018, as required by law, two key realities emerged. One, he was the first prime minister to convene a board meeting since the Act was passed, even though quarterly meetings were required. Two, the national coordinator at the time recommended that the prime minister dissolve the body, as it had no use or role in countering terrorism in the country.
This was the first and last board meeting held under the original Act. In July 2019, parliament amended it through an ordinance, which it later passed in March 2020. The amendment made the interior minister the board chairman and the national coordinator its secretary. Several references to the “prime minister” in the Act were also replaced, shifting Nacta’s reporting line to the interior ministry. The 2019-2020 amendments thus downgraded Nacta from a prime minister-led federal-provincial body to one under the interior minister. Interestingly, one of the few board meetings held since then, and chaired by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, approved the establishment of Niftac. Just before Niftac was introduced, Nacta inducted around 130 permanent officers. Since Niftac’s establishment, most have struggled to find a role.
Niftac was described as a national platform connecting more than 50 federal and provincial departments and agencies — supported by provincial fusion centres — to improve intelligence coordination, speed up threat assessment, and strengthen information-sharing across institutional boundaries. That was Nacta’s purpose.
A military or intelligence institution can possess information that a civilian authority cannot access. It can conduct operations a civilian institution cannot. It can assess threats from a classified perspective. But the state also needs an institution that can sit openly with provincial police, civil administration, prosecutors, courts, parliamentarians, researchers and international partners. It needs an institution whose authority is intelligible within the civilian legal and administrative system.
Against this backdrop, Niftac overshadowed Nacta. Even before Maj Gen Faisal Naseer was appointed national coordinator, Niftac and its officers from the superior security institutions appeared more assertive and powerful than the national coordinator.
In fact, Nacta, the only civilian-led CT body, struggled to find its role and eventually lost that struggle. Now the vision and implementation plan will flow top-down, and space for consultation, policy discourse, and debate will gradually vanish.
This institutional transformation is taking place at a time when Pakistan faces its worst terrorism challenge, one that is growing more complex by the day. The state is trying hard to find a way out of the menace, but these transformations will not solve it. Concentrating power in one set of hands can be challenging because absolute control centralises the burden.
The writer is a security analyst.
Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

topic: Counter-Terrorism Institutional Framework and Civil-Military Relations in Pakistan
whyMatters: This article critically analyzes the decline of a key civilian counter-terrorism body in Pakistan, Nacta, offering insights into institutional decay and the evolving civil-military dynamic in security policy. Aspirants can use it to discuss challenges in governance, counter-terrorism strategy, and the centralization of power in security institutions.
summary: Nacta, conceived in 2008 as a civilian counterterrorism body for policymaking, coordination, and data, failed to fully realize its mandate despite legal cover from the Nacta Act, 2013, due to persistent resistance from LEAs and superior security institutions.

The establishment of the National Intelligence Fusion and Threat Assessment Centre (Niftac) in 2025 (as per the article's timeline) as a parallel and effectively superior body superseded Nacta, thereby shifting the leading role in counterterrorism to a superior security institution.

Institutional transformations, including the National Security and War Course for bureaucrats and military-led courses for opinion-makers, aim to synchronize civilian-led LEAs with the military's security doctrine, gradually eroding space for independent civilian policy discourse.

Internal issues within the police cadre serving in Nacta, coupled with amendments in 2019-2020 that downgraded Nacta's reporting line from the Prime Minister to the Interior Minister, significantly contributed to its weakening and eventual loss of purpose.
facts: Nacta was conceived in December 2008 and gained legal cover under the Nacta Act, 2013.
The National Intelligence Fusion and Threat Assessment Centre (Niftac) was established in 2025 (as per the article), effectively superseding Nacta.
Prime Minister Imran Khan chaired the first Nacta board of governors meeting since the Act's passage in September 2018.
The Nacta Act was amended in July 2019 (ordinance) and passed in March 2020, shifting its reporting line from the Prime Minister to the Interior Ministry.
Around 130 permanent officers were inducted into Nacta just before Niftac's establishment, most of whom later struggled to find a role.
academicReferences: National Action Plan (NAP), 2014 - Pakistan's comprehensive strategy against terrorism and extremism, providing a foundational context for institutional roles.
National Security Policy of Pakistan (2022-2026) - Offers insight into the state's broader security doctrine and the intended roles of various institutions.

Ayesha Siddiqa's 'Military Inc.: Inside Pakistan's Military Economy' - Provides a critical analytical framework for understanding the military's expanding influence in state affairs, including security policy and institutional control.

quiz.question: Which body was originally conceived as a civilian counterterrorism institution combining policymaking, coordination, and data collection in Pakistan?
options: A) National Counter Terrorism Authority (Nacta)
B) National Intelligence Fusion and Threat Assessment Centre (Niftac)
C) Federal Investigation Agency (FIA)
D) National Defence University (NDU)
quiz.explanation: The article explicitly states that Nacta was "once conceived as a civilian counterterrorism body that combined policymaking, coordination among law-enforcement agencies, and data collection and processing."

quiz.question: According to the article, what significant amendment was made to the Nacta Act in 2019-2020?
options: A) It dissolved Nacta entirely and transferred its functions to Niftac.
B) It shifted the chairmanship of the Nacta board from the Prime Minister to the Interior Minister.
C) It mandated the National Coordinator to always be a senior military officer.
D) It expanded Nacta's operational role to include direct law enforcement activities.
quiz.explanation: The article mentions, "The amendment made the interior minister the board chairman and the national coordinator its secretary. Several references to the 'prime minister' in the Act were also replaced, shifting Nacta’s reporting line to the interior ministry."

quiz.question: What internal factor, besides external pressure, contributed to Nacta's downfall as highlighted in the article?
options: A) Lack of international funding for Nacta's projects.
B) The police cadre's internal destruction of the institution and provision of an excuse for its takeover.
C) Excessive bureaucracy preventing swift decision-making.
D) Inadequate legislative support from the parliament.
quiz.explanation: The article states, "Still, the police cadre is undoubtedly responsible for destroying the institution and providing an excuse for its takeover."

quiz.question: What is identified as the 'real purpose' behind Nacta's new form and broader institutional transformations concerning internal security policy?
options: A) To enhance independent civilian oversight of counterterrorism operations.
B) To centralize the burden of counterterrorism policymaking solely on the civilian government.
C) To synchronize civilian-led LEAs with the security doctrine conceived by the establishment’s top brass.
D) To establish Nacta as the sole operational counterterrorism body in the country.
quiz.explanation: The article states, "Its real purpose is to synchronise all civilian-led LEAs with the superior security institution, and, at the very least, to bring them under one roof."

flashcards.front: What was Nacta's original vision and its ultimate fate, according to the article?
flashcards.back: Nacta was conceived as a civilian counterterrorism body for policymaking, coordination, and data collection. It ultimately failed to realize its mandate and effectively 'lost' its role, being superseded by security institutions.

flashcards.front: How did the establishment of Niftac impact Nacta's statutory role and authority?
flashcards.back: Niftac was created as a parallel body, effectively superior to Nacta, granting a superior security institution the leading role and overshadowing Nacta, despite the latter being the statutory body.

flashcards.front: Beyond external pressures, what internal factor contributed significantly to Nacta's downfall as highlighted in the article?
flashcards.back: The police cadre's internal issues, including officers on deputation having little idea of Nacta's objectives, are cited as contributing to the institution's destruction and providing an excuse for its takeover.

flashcards.front: What broader institutional transformation is Nacta's decline symptomatic of, concerning Pakistan's internal security structure?
flashcards.back: Nacta's decline is symptomatic of a long-term process to synchronize civilian-led law enforcement agencies with the security doctrine conceived by the establishment's top brass, aiming at greater control and centralizing the burden of security policy.
